He expects to support his family by his trade, not by his lodgers, whereas in Paris and Edinburgh people who let lodgings commonly have no other means of subsistence, so the price of the lodging must cover not only the rent of the house but the whole expense of the family.
Part II: Inequalities caused by the Policy of Europe.

Such are the inequalities in the whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock that must arise from the absence of any of the three requisites mentioned above, even where there is the most perfect liberty. But the policy of Europe, by not leaving things at perfect liberty, causes other inequalities of far greater importance.

It does this chiefly in the three following ways. First, by restricting the competition in some employments to fewer people than would otherwise be willing to enter them. Second, by increasing it in others beyond what it would naturally be. And third, by obstructing the free movement of labour and stock, both from one employment to another and from one place to another.

First, the policy of Europe causes a very important inequality in the whole of the advantages and disadvantages of the different employments of labour and stock by restricting the competition in some employments to fewer people than might otherwise be willing to enter them.
The exclusive privileges granted to corporations are the main tool Europe uses to bring this about.

When a trade is incorporated and given an exclusive privilege, it automatically limits competition within the town to those who are free of the trade. To win that freedom, you normally have to serve an apprenticeship in the town under a master who is properly qualified. The corporation's bye-laws sometimes cap the number of apprentices any one master may take, and they almost always fix the number of years each apprentice must serve. Both rules aim at the same thing: to keep competition far smaller than the number of people who would otherwise want to enter the trade. Capping the number of apprentices limits it directly. A long apprenticeship limits it more indirectly, but just as effectively, by driving up the cost of training.

In Sheffield, a corporation bye-law forbids any master cutler from keeping more than one apprentice at a time. In Norfolk and Norwich, no master weaver may keep more than two apprentices, on pain of forfeiting five pounds a month to the king. No master hatter anywhere in England, or in the English plantations, may keep more than two apprentices, on pain of forfeiting five pounds a month, half to the king and half to whoever sues for it in a court of record. Both of these rules, though they have been confirmed by a public law of the kingdom, are plainly driven by the same corporation spirit that produced the Sheffield bye-law. The silk-weavers in London had barely been incorporated for a year before they passed a bye-law forbidding any master from keeping more than two apprentices at a time. It took a special act of parliament to repeal it.

All across Europe, seven years seems to have been the standard length of apprenticeship in most incorporated trades in earlier times. All such incorporations used to be called universities, which is in fact simply the Latin word for any incorporated body. The university of smiths, the university of tailors, and similar phrases turn up regularly in the old charters of ancient towns. When the particular incorporations we now specifically call universities were first founded, the number of years required to earn the degree of master of arts was plainly copied from the apprenticeship term in ordinary trades, whose incorporations were much older. Just as you had to work seven years under a properly qualified master before you could become a master yourself and take on apprentices in an ordinary trade, so you had to study seven years under a properly qualified master before you could become a master, teacher, or doctor (words that were once interchangeable) in the liberal arts, and take on scholars or apprentices (words that were also originally the same) to study under you.

Under the fifth year of Elizabeth's reign, in the law commonly called the Statute of Apprenticeship, it was enacted that from then on no one could practise any trade, craft, or skilled occupation then carried on in England unless he had first served an apprenticeship of at least seven years to it. What had previously been the bye-law of many individual corporations now became, in England, the general public law of every trade carried on in market towns. The words of the statute are very broad and seem clearly to cover the whole kingdom, but through legal interpretation its scope has been confined to market towns. The courts have held that in country villages a person may carry on several different trades without having served a seven-year apprenticeship to each, since those trades are needed for the convenience of the inhabitants and there are often too few people to supply each trade with its own set of hands. By a strict reading of the words, the statute has also been confined to trades already established in England before the fifth year of Elizabeth, and has never been extended to trades introduced since. This limit has produced several distinctions that, judged as rules of policy, are about as silly as anything could be. The courts have ruled, for instance, that a coach-maker may neither make his own coach-wheels nor employ journeymen to make them, but must buy them from a master wheelwright, because wheelwrighting was practised in England before the fifth year of Elizabeth. Yet a wheelwright, though he has never served an apprenticeship to a coach-maker, may make coaches himself or employ journeymen to make them, because coach-making does not fall under the statute, not having been practised in England when the statute was passed. Many of the manufactures of Manchester, Birmingham, and Wolverhampton fall outside the statute on the same grounds, since they were not practised in England before the fifth year of Elizabeth.

In France, the length of apprenticeship varies from town to town and from trade to trade. In Paris, five years is the term required in a great many trades; but in many of them, before anyone can qualify to practise the trade as a master, he must serve a further five years as a journeyman. During this second stretch he is called his master's companion, and the term itself is called his companionship.

In Scotland there is no general law that sets a uniform length for apprenticeships. The term varies from one corporation to another. Where it is long, part of it can usually be bought off by paying a small fine. In most towns, too, a very small fine is enough to buy the freedom of any corporation. The weavers of linen and hempen cloth, the country's main manufactures, along with all the other craftsmen who support them, such as wheel-makers and reel-makers, may practise their trades in any incorporated town without paying any fine. In every incorporated town, anyone is free to sell butcher's meat on any lawful day of the week. Three years is a common apprenticeship term in Scotland, even in some quite delicate trades, and overall I know of no country in Europe where corporation laws are so little oppressive.

The property each man has in his own labour is the original foundation of all other property, and it is also the most sacred and inviolable. A poor man's inheritance lies in the strength and skill of his hands, and to stop him from using that strength and skill however he sees fit, so long as he harms no neighbour, is a plain violation of this most sacred property. It is an obvious encroachment on the just liberty both of the workman and of anyone who might want to employ him. Just as it stops the one from working at what he chooses, it stops the others from employing whom they choose. Whether a man is fit to be employed can surely be left to the judgement of the employers, whose own interest is so closely involved. The lawmaker's affected concern that they might employ the wrong person is as meddlesome as it is oppressive.

Long apprenticeships are no guarantee that shoddy workmanship will not often be put up for public sale. When that happens, it is usually the result of fraud, not of incompetence, and the longest apprenticeship is no guard against fraud. Preventing that abuse calls for quite different regulations. The sterling mark on silver plate and the stamps on linen and woollen cloth give the buyer far more security than any apprenticeship statute. He normally checks these marks, but never thinks it worth asking whether the workman served a seven-year apprenticeship.

Long apprenticeships do nothing to make young people industrious. A journeyman paid by the piece is likely to work hard, because he gains from every bit of effort. An apprentice is likely to be idle, and almost always is, because he has no immediate stake in being otherwise. In the lower occupations, the rewards of labour consist entirely in the pay for it. Those who are soonest in a position to enjoy that pay are likely to develop a taste for work soonest, and to pick up the habit of industry early. A young man naturally comes to hate work when he gets nothing from it for a long stretch. The boys sent out as apprentices by public charities are usually bound for more than the usual number of years, and they usually turn out very idle and worthless.

Apprenticeships were entirely unknown to the ancients. The mutual duties of master and apprentice make up a substantial part of every modern legal code, yet Roman law says nothing at all about them. I know of no Greek or Latin word, and I think I can safely say there is none, that captures what we now mean by apprentice: a servant bound to work at a particular trade for a master's benefit, over a term of years, on the condition that the master teach him that trade.

Long apprenticeships are entirely unnecessary. The skilled crafts that stand well above ordinary trades, such as making clocks and watches, hold no mystery deep enough to require a long course of instruction. The original invention of such beautiful machines, and even of some of the tools used to make them, must of course have taken deep thought and long time, and rightly ranks among the finest achievements of human ingenuity. But once both have been properly invented and are well understood, explaining to any young man, in the fullest possible way, how to use the tools and how to build the machines need not take more than a few weeks of lessons; perhaps a few days would do. In the ordinary mechanical trades a few days would certainly be enough. Manual dexterity, even in ordinary trades, cannot be acquired without a great deal of practice and experience. But a young man would practise with far more diligence and care if from the start he worked as a journeyman, paid in proportion to the little he could produce, and paying in turn for the materials he might spoil now and then through clumsiness and inexperience. His training would generally be more effective this way, and always less tedious and less expensive. The master, it is true, would lose out. He would lose all the apprentice's wages that he now saves over seven years together. In the end the apprentice himself might lose out too. In a trade so easily learnt he would face more competitors, and his wages, once he became a finished workman, would be much lower than they are now. The same rise in competition would cut the masters' profits as well as the workmen's wages. The trades, the crafts, the skilled occupations would all be losers. But the public would gain, because the work of all these craftsmen would reach the market far cheaper.

It is to prevent this fall in price, and so in wages and profit, by suppressing the free competition that would certainly cause it, that all corporations and most corporation laws have been set up. In earlier times, in many parts of Europe, no authority was needed to create a corporation except that of the incorporated town where it was established. In England, admittedly, a charter from the king was also required. But this royal prerogative seems to have been kept up more as a way of squeezing money out of subjects than as a defence of common liberty against such oppressive monopolies. On payment of a fine to the king, the charter was generally granted readily enough; and when a particular group of craftsmen or traders chose to act as a corporation without a charter, such bodies, called adulterine guilds, were not always stripped of their privileges on that account, but were merely required to pay the king an annual fine for permission to exercise their usurped rights (see Madox, Firma Burgi, p. 26 and following). Direct oversight of all corporations, and of any bye-laws they chose to enact for their own governance, belonged to the incorporated town where they were based; and whatever discipline was applied to them came, as a rule, not from the king, but from that larger incorporated body of which these lesser ones were only parts or members.

The government of incorporated towns lay entirely in the hands of traders and craftsmen, and it was plainly in the interest of each particular group of them to keep the market from being overstocked, as they usually put it, with its own kind of work, which really means keeping it permanently understocked. Each group was eager to set up regulations to serve this purpose and, provided it was allowed to do so, was happy to let every other group do the same. As a result of such regulations, each group did have to buy the goods it needed from every other group in the town at somewhat higher prices than it might otherwise have paid. But in return it could sell its own goods at correspondingly higher prices; so on that score it came out about even, as the saying goes, and in their dealings with one another none of the different groups within the town lost anything by these regulations. In their dealings with the countryside, however, they all gained greatly, and it is in these latter dealings that the whole trade which supports and enriches every town consists.

Every town draws its entire subsistence, and all the raw materials for its industry, from the countryside. It pays for these mainly in two ways. First, by sending part of those materials back to the country worked up and manufactured; in which case their price is raised by the wages of the workmen and the profits of their masters or direct employers. Second, by sending the country a portion of the raw and manufactured produce of other countries, or of distant parts of the same country, that has been imported into the town; in which case the original price of those goods is likewise raised by the wages of the carriers or sailors and by the profits of the merchants who employ them. The gain on the first of these branches of commerce is the advantage the town makes from its manufactures; the gain on the second is the advantage of its inland and foreign trade. The wages of the workmen and the profits of their various employers make up the whole of what is gained on both. Any regulation, therefore, that raises those wages and profits above what they would otherwise be lets the town buy the produce of a greater quantity of country labour with a smaller quantity of its own. It gives the traders and craftsmen of the town an advantage over the landlords, farmers, and labourers of the country, and destroys the natural equality that would otherwise hold in the commerce carried on between them. The whole annual produce of the society's labour is divided each year between these two different sets of people. By means of such regulations, a larger share of it goes to the townspeople than would otherwise fall to them, and a smaller share to the country.

The price a town really pays for the provisions and materials imported into it each year is the quantity of manufactures and other goods it exports each year. The dearer it sells the latter, the cheaper it buys the former. The town's industry becomes more advantageous, the country's less so.

We do not need fine calculations to convince ourselves that town industry is everywhere in Europe more advantageous than country industry; one simple, obvious observation will do. In every European country we find at least a hundred people who have made great fortunes from small beginnings through trade and manufactures, the industry that properly belongs to towns, for every one who has done so through the industry that properly belongs to the country, the raising of raw produce by improving and cultivating land. Industry must therefore be better rewarded, and the wages of labour and the profits of stock must clearly be higher, in the one setting than in the other. But stock and labour naturally seek out the most advantageous employment. They therefore flock as much as they can to the town and abandon the country.

Because townspeople are gathered together in one place, they can easily combine. So even the most trivial trades carried on in towns have, somewhere or other, been incorporated; and even where they never have been, the corporation spirit, the suspicion of outsiders, the reluctance to take apprentices or to share the secrets of the trade, generally prevails, and often teaches them, through voluntary associations and agreements, to block the free competition they cannot forbid by bye-law. The trades that employ only a few hands slide most easily into such combinations. Perhaps half a dozen wool-combers are needed to keep a thousand spinners and weavers at work. By agreeing not to take apprentices, they can not only monopolise the work but reduce the whole manufacture to a kind of slavery under them, and push the price of their labour far above what the nature of their work warrants.

Country people, scattered across distant places, cannot easily combine. Not only have they never been incorporated, but the corporation spirit has never taken hold among them. No apprenticeship has ever been thought necessary to qualify a man for farming, the great trade of the country. Yet apart from what are called the fine arts and the liberal professions, there is perhaps no trade that demands so great a variety of knowledge and experience. The countless volumes written on it in every language may convince us that even among the wisest and most learned nations it has never been seen as a thing easily understood. And from all those volumes we shall try in vain to extract the knowledge of its many complicated operations that even the ordinary farmer commonly possesses, however contemptuously the very contemptible authors of some of them may sometimes speak of him. By contrast, there is hardly any common mechanical trade whose every operation cannot be explained as fully and clearly as words and diagrams allow in a pamphlet of just a few pages. In the history of the arts now being published by the French Academy of Sciences, several of them are in fact explained in exactly this way. What is more, directing operations that must be adjusted with every change in the weather, and with many other accidents besides, calls for far more judgement and discretion than directing operations that are always, or very nearly, the same.

Not only the farmer's art, the general direction of farming operations, but many lesser branches of country labour demand far more skill and experience than most mechanical trades. The man who works in brass and iron works with tools, and on materials, whose temper is always the same, or nearly so. But the man who ploughs the ground with a team of horses or oxen works with tools whose health, strength, and temper vary greatly from one occasion to the next. The condition of the materials he works on is as variable as that of the tools he works with, and both must be handled with much judgement and discretion. The common ploughman, though generally taken as the very model of stupidity and ignorance, is seldom lacking in this judgement and discretion. He is less used to social company, it is true, than the mechanic who lives in a town. His voice and speech are rougher and harder to follow for those not used to them. But his understanding, accustomed to weighing a greater variety of objects, is generally much superior to that of the townsman, whose whole attention from morning to night is usually taken up with one or two very simple operations. Anyone whom business or curiosity has led to talk much with both knows well how far the lower ranks of country people really surpass those of the town. In China and Hindustan, accordingly, both the standing and the wages of country labourers are said to be higher than those of most craftsmen and manufacturers. They would probably be so everywhere if corporation laws and the corporation spirit did not prevent it.

The advantage that town industry enjoys everywhere in Europe over country industry is not entirely due to corporations and corporation laws. It is propped up by many other regulations too. The heavy duties on foreign manufactures, and on all goods imported by foreign merchants, all serve the same end. Corporation laws let townspeople raise their prices without fear of being undersold by the free competition of their own countrymen. Those other regulations protect them just as well against the competition of foreigners. The price increase caused by both is in the end always paid by the landlords, farmers, and labourers of the country, who have seldom opposed the setting up of such monopolies. They usually have neither the inclination nor the aptitude to form combinations; and the noise and clever arguments of merchants and manufacturers easily persuade them that the private interest of one part of society, and a subordinate part at that, is the general interest of the whole.

In Great Britain, town industry seems to have held a greater advantage over country industry in former times than it does now. The wages of country labour come nearer to those of manufacturing labour, and the profits of stock employed in farming nearer to those of stock employed in trade and manufacture, than they are said to have done in the last century or at the start of the present one. This change may be seen as the necessary, though very late, consequence of the extraordinary encouragement given to town industry. The stocks built up in towns grow so large in time that they can no longer be employed at the old profit in the kind of industry peculiar to towns. That industry, like every other, has its limits; and as stock grows, the increased competition necessarily drives down profit. The fall in town profit pushes stock out into the country, where, by creating fresh demand for country labour, it necessarily raises country wages. The stock then spreads, if I may put it so, over the face of the land, and, by being employed in farming, is partly returned to the country at whose expense it had largely been built up in the town in the first place. I shall try later to show that everywhere in Europe the greatest improvements of the countryside have come from such overflowings of stock originally accumulated in the towns, and at the same time to show that although some countries have by this route reached a considerable degree of wealth, the process is necessarily slow, uncertain, easily disturbed and interrupted by countless accidents, and in every respect contrary to the order of nature and of reason. The interests, prejudices, laws, and customs that have given rise to it I shall try to explain as fully and clearly as I can in the third and fourth books of this inquiry.

People in the same trade seldom meet together, even for fun and recreation, without the conversation ending in a conspiracy against the public, or in some scheme to raise prices. It is impossible, of course, to prevent such meetings by any law that could either be enforced or be consistent with liberty and justice. But although the law cannot stop people in the same trade from gathering now and then, it should do nothing to make such gatherings easier, still less to make them necessary.

A regulation that requires everyone in the same trade in a particular town to register their names and addresses in a public record makes such gatherings easier. It links up individuals who might otherwise never have known each other, and tells every man in the trade where to find every other.

A regulation that lets people in the same trade tax themselves in order to provide for their poor, their sick, their widows and orphans, gives them a common interest to manage and so makes such gatherings necessary.

Incorporation not only makes such gatherings necessary but makes the decision of the majority binding on everyone. In a free trade, an effective combination can be set up only by the unanimous agreement of every single trader, and it can last only as long as every single trader stays of the same mind. The majority of a corporation, by contrast, can pass a bye-law with proper penalties that will limit competition more effectively and more lastingly than any voluntary combination ever could.

The claim that corporations are needed for the better governance of a trade has no foundation. The real and effective discipline a workman is subject to comes not from his corporation but from his customers. It is the fear of losing their custom that checks his frauds and corrects his carelessness. An exclusive corporation necessarily weakens this discipline. A fixed set of workmen then has to be employed, whether they behave well or badly. That is why, in many large incorporated towns, no decent workmen can be found even in some of the most essential trades. If you want your work done at all well, it has to be done in the suburbs, where the workmen, having no exclusive privilege, have nothing to rely on but their reputation, and then you must smuggle it into the town as best you can.

It is in this way that the policy of Europe, by restricting competition in certain occupations to fewer people than would otherwise want to enter them, creates a very significant inequality across the whole range of advantages and disadvantages in the different employments of labour and stock.

Secondly, the policy of Europe, by raising competition in certain occupations above its natural level, creates another inequality, of the opposite kind, across the whole range of advantages and disadvantages in the different employments of labour and stock.

It has been thought so important that a proper number of young people be trained for certain professions that sometimes the state, and sometimes the piety of private founders, has set up many pensions, scholarships, exhibitions, bursaries, and the like for the purpose, which draw far more people into those professions than could otherwise hope to follow them. In every Christian country, I believe, the education of most clergymen is paid for in this way. Very few of them are educated entirely at their own expense. So the long, tedious, and expensive education of those who are will not always earn them a fitting reward, since the church is crowded with people who, in order to get a post, are willing to accept a much smaller payment than their education would otherwise have entitled them to; and in this way the competition of the poor strips the rich of their reward. It would be improper, no doubt, to compare a curate or a chaplain with a journeyman in any ordinary trade. Yet the pay of a curate or chaplain may fairly be regarded as the same in nature as a journeyman's wages. All three are paid for their work according to whatever contract they happen to make with their respective superiors. Until after the middle of the fourteenth century, five marks, containing about as much silver as ten pounds of our present money, was the usual pay in England for a curate or a stipendiary parish priest, as we find it fixed by the decrees of several different national councils. In the same period, fourpence a day, containing the same quantity of silver as a shilling of our present money, was declared to be the pay of a master mason, and threepence a day, equal to ninepence of our present money, that of a journeyman mason (see the Statute of Labourers, 25 Edward III). The wages of both these labourers, then, assuming they were kept constantly employed, were much higher than the curate's. Even if the master mason had been out of work a third of the year, his wages would still have fully matched the curate's. By the twelfth year of Queen Anne, chapter 12, it is declared that "whereas, for want of sufficient maintenance and encouragement to curates, the cures have, in several places, been meanly supplied, the bishop is, therefore, empowered to appoint, by writing under his hand and seal, a sufficient certain stipend or allowance, not exceeding fifty, and not less than twenty pounds a-year." Forty pounds a year is now reckoned very good pay for a curate; and despite this act of parliament, there are many curacies worth less than twenty pounds a year. There are journeyman shoemakers in London who earn forty pounds a year, and there is hardly a hard-working tradesman of any kind in that city who does not earn more than twenty. That last figure, indeed, is no more than what common labourers often earn in many country parishes. Whenever the law has tried to regulate workmen's wages, it has always been to lower them rather than to raise them. But on many occasions the law has tried to raise curates' wages, and, for the dignity of the church, to force parish rectors to pay them more than the wretched maintenance the curates themselves would be willing to take. In both cases the law has proved equally useless, and has never managed either to raise curates' wages or to push labourers' wages down to the intended level; because it has never been able to stop the curate from being willing to take less than the legal allowance, given the poverty of his situation and the throng of his competitors, or to stop the labourer from getting more, given the opposing competition of those who hoped to gain either profit or pleasure from employing him.

The great benefices and other church dignities uphold the honour of the church, despite the meagre circumstances of some of its lower members. The respect paid to the profession also makes some amends, even to them, for the poverty of their pay. In England, and in all Roman Catholic countries, the lottery of the church is in fact far more rewarding than it needs to be. The example of the churches of Scotland, of Geneva, and of several other Protestant churches may convince us that in so respectable a profession, where education is so easily obtained, the prospect of much more modest benefices will draw enough learned, decent, and respectable men into holy orders.

In professions that have no benefices, such as law and medicine, if an equal proportion of people were educated at public expense, competition would soon grow so fierce as to drive their pay right down. It might then not be worth any man's while to pay for his son's training in either profession out of his own pocket. They would be left entirely to those educated by such public charities, whose numbers and poverty would generally force them to settle for a very miserable reward, completely degrading the now respectable professions of law and medicine.

That luckless breed of men commonly called men of letters are pretty much in the position lawyers and physicians would be in under the supposition just made. In every part of Europe, most of them were educated for the church, but were kept from entering holy orders for one reason or another. They have therefore generally been educated at public expense; and their numbers are everywhere so great as commonly to drive the price of their labour down to a very paltry reward.

Before the invention of printing, the only way a man of letters could earn anything by his talents was as a public or private teacher, by passing on to others the curious and useful knowledge he had gained himself; and this is surely still a more honourable, a more useful, and generally even a more profitable occupation than the other one printing has given rise to, writing for a bookseller. The time and study, the genius, knowledge, and application needed to make an eminent teacher of the sciences are at least equal to what the greatest practitioners of law and medicine require. But the usual reward of the eminent teacher bears no comparison to that of the lawyer or physician, because the teacher's profession is crowded with poor people who were brought up to it at public expense, whereas the other two are burdened with very few who were not educated at their own. Even the usual pay of public and private teachers, small as it may seem, would no doubt be smaller still if the competition of those still more destitute men of letters who write for a living were not kept out of the market. Before printing was invented, a scholar and a beggar seem to have been almost interchangeable terms. The various heads of universities, before that time, appear often to have granted their scholars licences to beg.

In ancient times, before any charities of this kind had been set up to educate poor people for the learned professions, the rewards of eminent teachers appear to have been far greater. Isocrates, in what is called his discourse against the sophists, reproaches the teachers of his own day with inconsistency. "They make the most magnificent promises to their scholars," he says, "and undertake to teach them to be wise, to be happy, and to be just; and, in return for so important a service, they stipulate the paltry reward of four or five minae." "Those who teach wisdom," he goes on, "ought certainly to be wise themselves; but if any man were to sell such a bargain for such a price, he would be convicted of the most evident folly." He certainly does not mean here to overstate the reward, and we may be sure it was no less than he says. Four minae came to thirteen pounds six shillings and eightpence; five minae to sixteen pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence. So something not less than the larger of those two sums must at that time have been the usual pay of the most eminent teachers at Athens. Isocrates himself charged ten minae, or 33 pounds 6 shillings 8 pence, from each scholar. When he taught at Athens he is said to have had a hundred scholars. I take this to be the number he taught at one time, or who attended what we would call one course of lectures; a number that will not seem extraordinary for so great a city and so famous a teacher, who taught, what is more, what was then the most fashionable of all subjects, rhetoric. He must therefore have made, from each course of lectures, a thousand minae, or 3,335 pounds 6 shillings 8 pence. A thousand minae is in fact named by Plutarch, in another passage, as his didactron, or usual fee for teaching. Many other eminent teachers of those times appear to have amassed great fortunes. Gorgias made a present to the temple of Delphi of a statue of himself in solid gold. We must not, I suppose, imagine it was life-size. His manner of living, like that of Hippias and Protagoras, two other eminent teachers of the time, is portrayed by Plato as splendid, even to the point of ostentation. Plato himself is said to have lived with a good deal of magnificence. Aristotle, after serving as tutor to Alexander, and being most generously rewarded, as everyone agrees, by both him and his father Philip, still thought it worth his while to return to Athens to take up teaching at his school again. Teachers of the sciences were probably less common in those days than they became an age or two later, when competition had probably somewhat reduced both the price of their labour and the admiration for their persons. Yet the most eminent of them seem always to have enjoyed a standing far above any of their profession today. The Athenians sent Carneades the Academic and Diogenes the Stoic on a solemn embassy to Rome; and although their city had by then declined from its former greatness, it was still an independent and considerable republic.

Carneades, moreover, was a Babylonian by birth; and since no people was ever more reluctant to admit foreigners to public office than the Athenians, the regard they showed him must have been very great.

On the whole, this inequality is perhaps more beneficial than harmful to the public. It may somewhat lower the standing of the public teacher; but the cheapness of education is surely an advantage that far outweighs this small drawback. The public might draw even greater benefit from it if the constitution of the schools and colleges where education is carried on were more sensible than it is at present across most of Europe.

Thirdly, the policy of Europe, by blocking the free movement of labour and stock, both from one employment to another and from one place to another, creates in some cases a very awkward inequality across the whole range of advantages and disadvantages in their different employments.

The Statute of Apprenticeship blocks the free movement of labour from one employment to another, even within the same place. The exclusive privileges of corporations block its movement from one place to another, even within the same employment.

It often happens that while high wages are paid to the workmen in one manufacture, those in another must make do with bare subsistence. The first is in a rising state and so has a constant demand for new hands; the second is in decline, and its surplus of hands keeps growing. These two manufactures may sometimes be in the same town, sometimes even in the same neighbourhood, without being able to give one another the least relief. The Statute of Apprenticeship may bar it in the one case, and both that and an exclusive corporation in the other. Yet in many different manufactures the operations are so alike that the workmen could easily switch trades with one another, if those absurd laws did not stop them. The crafts of weaving plain linen and plain silk, for instance, are almost identical. Weaving plain woollen is somewhat different, but the difference is so slight that either a linen or a silk weaver could become a passable workman in a very few days. So if any of those three major manufactures were declining, the workmen could fall back on whichever of the other two was in a more flourishing state; and their wages would neither rise too high in the thriving trade nor sink too low in the failing one. The linen manufacture, it is true, is open to everyone in England by a particular statute; but since it is not much pursued through most of the country, it offers no general refuge to the workmen of other declining manufactures, who, wherever the Statute of Apprenticeship applies, have no choice but to fall on the parish or work as common labourers, for which their habits make them far less suited than for any manufacture resembling their own. So they generally choose to fall on the parish.

Whatever blocks the free movement of labour from one employment to another blocks that of stock as well, since the quantity of stock that can be used in any branch of business depends very much on the quantity of labour that can be used in it. Corporation laws, however, hinder the free movement of stock from place to place less than they hinder that of labour. Everywhere it is much easier for a wealthy merchant to obtain the right to trade in an incorporated town than for a poor craftsman to obtain the right to work in it.

The hindrance that corporation laws place on the free movement of labour is common, I believe, to every part of Europe. The hindrance placed on it by the poor laws is, as far as I know, peculiar to England. It lies in the difficulty a poor man finds in gaining a settlement, or even in being allowed to practise his trade in any parish but the one he belongs to. Corporation laws obstruct the free movement only of craftsmen and manufacturers. The difficulty of gaining settlements obstructs even that of common labour. It may be worth giving some account of the rise, progress, and present state of this disorder, perhaps the greatest of any in the policing of England.

When the destruction of the monasteries deprived the poor of the charity of those religious houses, and after some other ineffective attempts to relieve them, it was enacted, by the forty-third year of Elizabeth, chapter 2, that every parish should be obliged to provide for its own poor, and that overseers of the poor should be appointed each year who, together with the churchwardens, should raise adequate sums for the purpose through a parish rate.

By this statute, the duty of providing for their own poor was firmly imposed on every parish. Who counted as the poor of each parish therefore became a question of some importance. After some variation, this question was finally settled by the thirteenth and fourteenth years of Charles II, when it was enacted that forty days of undisturbed residence should gain anyone a settlement in any parish; but that within that time, on a complaint by the churchwardens or overseers of the poor, two justices of the peace could remove any new resident to the parish where he was last legally settled, unless he either rented a property worth ten pounds a year or could give such security against any charge to the parish where he was then living as the justices judged sufficient.

Some frauds, it is said, followed from this statute, parish officers sometimes bribing their own poor to slip off quietly to another parish and, by keeping out of sight for forty days, gain a settlement there, relieving the parish they really belonged to. So it was enacted, by the first year of James II, that the forty days of undisturbed residence needed to gain a settlement should be counted only from the time a person gave written notice, to one of the churchwardens or overseers of the parish he came to live in, of his address and the size of his family.

But parish officers, it seems, were not always more honest about their own poor than they had been about those of other parishes, and sometimes turned a blind eye to such intrusions, accepting the notice and then taking no proper steps in response. Since every person in a parish was supposed to have an interest in preventing as far as possible their being burdened by such intruders, it was further enacted, by the third year of William III, that the forty days of residence should be counted only from the reading out of such written notice in church on a Sunday, immediately after divine service.

"After all," says Doctor Burn, "this kind of settlement, by continuing forty days after publication of notice in writing, is very seldom obtained; and the design of the acts is not so much for gaining of settlements, as for the avoiding of them by persons coming into a parish clandestinely, for the giving of notice is only putting a force upon the parish to remove. But if a person's situation is such, that it is doubtful whether he is actually removable or not, he shall, by giving of notice, compel the parish either to allow him a settlement uncontested, by suffering him to continue forty days, or by removing him to try the right."

This statute, then, made it almost impossible for a poor man to gain a new settlement the old way, by forty days of residence. But so as not to seem to shut off the common people of one parish from ever settling securely in another, it laid down four other ways a settlement might be gained without any notice given or published. The first was by being assessed for parish rates and paying them; the second, by being elected to an annual parish office and serving in it for a year; the third, by serving an apprenticeship in the parish; the fourth, by being hired into service there for a year and staying in the same service throughout it. No one can gain a settlement by either of the first two ways except by the public act of the whole parish, who know the consequences too well to take on any newcomer with nothing but his labour to support him, whether by assessing him for parish rates or by electing him to a parish office.

No married man can well gain a settlement by either of the last two ways. An apprentice is hardly ever married; and it is expressly enacted that no married servant shall gain a settlement by being hired for a year. The main effect of introducing settlement by service has been largely to do away with the old custom of hiring for a year, which had once been so usual in England that even now, if no particular term is agreed, the law assumes every servant is hired for a year. But masters are not always willing to give their servants a settlement by hiring them this way; and servants are not always willing to be hired this way, because, since every new settlement cancels all earlier ones, they might thereby lose their original settlement in their birthplace, the home of their parents and relations.

Clearly no independent workman, whether labourer or craftsman, is likely to gain a new settlement either by apprenticeship or by service. So when such a man took his trade to a new parish, he was liable to be removed, however healthy and hard-working he might be, at the whim of any churchwarden or overseer, unless he either rented a property worth ten pounds a year, an impossibility for someone with nothing but his labour to live on, or could give such security against any charge to the parish as two justices of the peace judged sufficient.

What security they may demand is, in fact, left entirely to their discretion; but they can hardly demand less than thirty pounds, since it has been enacted that the purchase even of a freehold estate worth less than thirty pounds shall not gain anyone a settlement, as being insufficient to indemnify the parish. But this is a security scarcely any man who lives by labour can give, and far greater security is often demanded.

To restore, in some measure, the free movement of labour that these various statutes had almost entirely taken away, the device of certificates was hit upon. By the eighth and ninth years of William III, it was enacted that if anyone brought a certificate from the parish where he was last legally settled, signed by the churchwardens and overseers of the poor and approved by two justices of the peace, every other parish should be obliged to receive him; that he should not be removable merely on the grounds that he was likely to become a charge, but only once he actually became one; and that the parish which granted the certificate should then be obliged to pay the cost both of his maintenance and of his removal. And to give the fullest possible security to the parish where such a certificated man came to live, the same statute further enacted that he should gain no settlement there by any means whatever, except by renting a property worth ten pounds a year or by serving on his own account in an annual parish office for one whole year; and so neither by notice, nor by service, nor by apprenticeship, nor by paying parish rates. By the twelfth year of Queen Anne, statute 1, chapter 18, it was further enacted that neither the servants nor the apprentices of such a certificated man should gain any settlement in the parish where he lived under such a certificate.

How far this device has restored the free movement of labour that the earlier statutes had almost entirely taken away we may judge from the following very shrewd remark of Doctor Burn. "It is obvious," he says, "that there are divers good reasons for requiring certificates with persons coming to settle in any place; namely, that persons residing under them can gain no settlement, neither by apprenticeship, nor by service, nor by giving notice, nor by paying parish rates; that they can settle neither apprentices nor servants; that if they become chargeable, it is certainly known whither to remove them, and the parish shall be paid for the removal, and for their maintenance in the mean time; and that, if they fall sick, and cannot be removed, the parish which gave the certificate must maintain them; none of all which can be without a certificate. Which reasons will hold proportionably for parishes not granting certificates in ordinary cases; for it is far more than an equal chance, but that they will have the certificated persons again, and in a worse condition." The moral of this observation seems to be that certificates ought always to be required by the parish a poor man comes to live in, and ought very seldom to be granted by the one he means to leave. "There is somewhat of hardship in this matter of certificates," says the same very intelligent author, in his History of the Poor Laws, "by putting it in the power of a parish officer to imprison a man as it were for life, however inconvenient it may be for him to continue at that place where he has had the misfortune to acquire what is called a settlement, or whatever advantage he may propose himself by living elsewhere."

Though a certificate carries no testimony of good behaviour, and certifies nothing but that the person belongs to the parish he really does belong to, it is entirely up to the parish officers whether to grant or refuse it. A mandamus was once moved for, says Doctor Burn, to compel the churchwardens and overseers to sign a certificate; but the Court of King's Bench rejected the motion as a very strange attempt.

The very uneven price of labour we often find in England, in places not far apart, is probably due to the obstruction that the law of settlements puts in the way of a poor man who would carry his trade from one parish to another without a certificate. A single man, if healthy and hard-working, may sometimes be allowed to stay without one; but a man with a wife and family who tried to do so would, in most parishes, be sure of being removed; and if the single man later married, he too would generally be removed. So a shortage of hands in one parish cannot always be relieved by a surplus in another, as it constantly is in Scotland, and, I believe, in every other country where settlement is no difficulty. In such countries, wages may sometimes rise a little near a great town, or wherever else there is an unusual demand for labour, and sink gradually as the distance from such places grows, until they drop back to the country's common rate; but we never meet those sudden, unaccountable differences in the wages of neighbouring places that we sometimes find in England, where it is often harder for a poor man to cross the artificial boundary of a parish than an arm of the sea or a ridge of high mountains, natural boundaries that sometimes mark off very distinctly different rates of wages in other countries.

To remove a man who has committed no offence from the parish where he chooses to live is a plain violation of natural liberty and justice. Yet the common people of England, so jealous of their liberty, but, like the common people of most countries, never quite grasping what it consists in, have now for more than a century allowed themselves to be exposed to this oppression without any remedy. Though thoughtful men have sometimes complained of the law of settlements as a public grievance, it has never become the target of any general popular outcry, like the outcry against general warrants, an abusive practice no doubt, but one not likely to cause any widespread oppression. I will venture to say there is hardly a poor man in England, forty years of age, who has not at some point in his life felt himself most cruelly oppressed by this ill-contrived law of settlements.

I shall close this long chapter by noting that, although in earlier times it was usual to fix wages, first by general laws covering the whole kingdom and later by particular orders of the justices of the peace in each county, both practices have now fallen completely out of use. "By the experience of above four hundred years," says Doctor Burn, "it seems time to lay aside all endeavours to bring under strict regulations, what in its own nature seems incapable of minute limitation; for if all persons in the same kind of work were to receive equal wages, there would be no emulation, and no room left for industry or ingenuity."

Particular acts of parliament, however, still sometimes try to regulate wages in particular trades and particular places. The eighth year of George III, for instance, forbids, under heavy penalties, all master tailors in London and within five miles of it from giving, and their workmen from accepting, more than two shillings and sevenpence halfpenny a day, except in a time of general mourning. Whenever the legislature tries to settle disputes between masters and their workmen, its advisers are always the masters. So when the regulation favours the workmen, it is always fair and equitable; but it is sometimes otherwise when it favours the masters. Thus the law that obliges the masters in several different trades to pay their workmen in money, not in goods, is quite fair and equitable. It imposes no real hardship on the masters. It only obliges them to pay in money the value they pretended to pay, but did not always really pay, in goods. That law favours the workmen; but the eighth of George III favours the masters. When masters combine to cut their workmen's wages, they commonly enter into a private bond or agreement not to give more than a certain wage, under a certain penalty. If the workmen were to enter into an opposite combination of the same kind, not to accept less than a certain wage, under a certain penalty, the law would punish them very severely; and if it dealt fairly, it would treat the masters the same way. But the eighth of George III enforces by law the very regulation that masters sometimes try to set up by such combinations. The workmen's complaint, that it puts the ablest and most industrious on the same footing as an ordinary workman, seems perfectly well founded.

In ancient times, too, it was usual to try to regulate the profits of merchants and other dealers by regulating the price of provisions and other goods. The assize of bread is, as far as I know, the only remnant of this ancient practice. Where there is an exclusive corporation, it may perhaps be proper to regulate the price of the first necessary of life; but where there is none, competition will regulate it far better than any assize. The method of fixing the assize of bread laid down by the thirty-first of George II could not be put into practice in Scotland, because of a defect in the law, its enforcement depending on the office of clerk of the market, which does not exist there. This defect was not remedied until the third of George III. The lack of an assize caused no noticeable inconvenience; and setting one up in the few places where it has so far been done has produced no noticeable benefit. In most of the towns of Scotland, however, there is an incorporation of bakers who claim exclusive privileges, though these are not very strictly guarded. The proportion between the different rates of wages and of profit in the different employments of labour and stock seems not to be much affected, as already noted, by the wealth or poverty, or the advancing, stationary, or declining state, of the society. Such upheavals in the public condition, though they affect the general rates both of wages and of profit, must in the end affect them equally across all the different employments. So the proportion between them must stay the same, and cannot well be altered, at least for any length of time, by any such upheavals.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: The Rent of Land

Rent, understood as the price paid for the use of land, is naturally the highest sum the tenant can manage to pay given the land's actual condition. When the terms of a lease are worked out, the landlord tries to leave the tenant no larger share of the produce than what will keep up the capital he draws his seed from, pay for the labour, and buy and maintain the cattle and other farming equipment, along with the ordinary profits that farming capital earns in that neighbourhood. That is plainly the smallest share the tenant can settle for without taking a loss, and the landlord rarely intends to leave him any more. Whatever portion of the produce, or what comes to the same thing, whatever portion of its price, exceeds this share, the landlord naturally tries to keep for himself as the rent of his land, and that is clearly the most the tenant can afford to pay given the land's actual condition. Sometimes the landlord's generosity, and more often his ignorance, leads him to accept somewhat less than this portion; and sometimes too, though more rarely, the tenant's ignorance leads him to agree to pay somewhat more, or to make do with somewhat less, than the ordinary profits of farming capital in the neighbourhood. Even so, this portion can still be regarded as the natural rent of land, the rent at which land is naturally meant, for the most part, to be let.

You might suppose that the rent of land is often nothing more than a reasonable profit or interest on the capital the landlord has spent improving it. On some occasions that may be partly true, but it can scarcely ever be more than partly true. The landlord demands a rent even for unimproved land, and the supposed interest or profit on the cost of improvement is generally added on top of this original rent. Besides, those improvements are not always made with the landlord's capital; sometimes they are made with the tenant's. Yet when the lease comes up for renewal, the landlord commonly demands the same increase in rent as if he had made all the improvements himself.

Sometimes he demands rent for something entirely beyond any human power to improve. Kelp is a kind of seaweed which, when burned, yields an alkaline salt useful for making glass and soap and for several other purposes. It grows in several parts of Great Britain, especially in Scotland, only on rocks that lie within the high-water mark, which are covered by the sea twice a day, so that its yield was never increased by any human effort. Yet the landlord whose estate borders a kelp shore of this sort demands a rent for it just as he does for his cornfields.

The sea around the Shetland islands is unusually rich in fish, which make up a large part of what the inhabitants live on. But to make use of what the water yields, they need a dwelling on the nearby land. The landlord's rent is set in proportion not to what the farmer can earn from the land alone, but to what he can earn from the land and the water together. Part of it is paid in sea-fish, and that country provides one of the very few cases in which rent forms part of the price of that commodity.

The rent of land, then, considered as the price paid for the use of the land, is naturally a monopoly price. It bears no relation at all to what the landlord may have spent improving the land, or to what he could afford to accept, but only to what the farmer can afford to give.

Only those parts of the land's produce can ordinarily be brought to market whose usual price is enough to cover the capital that must be used to bring them there, along with its ordinary profits. If the usual price is more than this, the surplus naturally goes to the rent of the land. If it is no more, the commodity can be brought to market but yields the landlord no rent. Whether the price is more or not depends on demand.

For some parts of the land's produce, the demand must always be high enough to yield a price greater than what is needed to bring them to market; for others, the demand may or may not be high enough to yield this greater price. The first kind must always yield a rent to the landlord. The second kind sometimes does and sometimes does not, depending on the circumstances.

Notice, then, that rent enters into the price of commodities in a different way from wages and profit. High or low wages and profit are the cause of high or low prices; high or low rent is the result of them. A commodity's price is high or low because high or low wages and profit must be paid to bring it to market. But it yields a high rent, a low rent, or no rent at all because its price is a great deal more, or only a little more, or no more, than what is enough to pay those wages and profit.

This chapter will fall into three parts, taking up: first, those parts of the land's produce that always yield some rent; second, those that sometimes do and sometimes do not yield rent; and third, the variations that naturally occur, at different stages of improvement, in the relative value of these two different kinds of raw produce, compared both with each other and with manufactured goods.
Part I. — Of the Produce of Land which always affords Rent.

Since men, like all other animals, naturally multiply in proportion to the means of supporting them, there is always more or less demand for food. Food can always buy or command a greater or smaller quantity of labour, and someone can always be found willing to do something to get it. The quantity of labour it can buy is not always equal to what it could support if managed in the most economical way, because labour is sometimes paid high wages; but food can always buy as much labour as it can support, at the rate at which that kind of labour is commonly supported in the neighbourhood.

But land, in almost any setting, produces more food than is enough to support all the labour needed to bring it to market, even in the most generous way in which that labour is ever supported. The surplus is also always more than enough to replace the capital that employed that labour, along with its profits. So something always remains as a rent for the landlord.

The most barren moors in Norway and Scotland produce some kind of pasture for cattle, whose milk and offspring are always more than enough not only to support all the labour of tending them and to pay the farmer or the owner of the herd or flock his ordinary profit, but also to yield the landlord some small rent. The rent rises in proportion to how good the pasture is. The same area of ground not only feeds more cattle, but because they are kept within a smaller space, less labour is needed to tend them and gather what they produce. The landlord gains in both ways: from the larger produce, and from the smaller amount of labour that must be supported out of it.

The rent of land varies not only with its fertility, whatever its produce, but also with its location, whatever its fertility. Land near a town yields a higher rent than equally fertile land in a distant part of the country. Cultivating the one may cost no more labour than the other, but it always costs more to bring the produce of the distant land to market. So more labour must be supported out of it, and the surplus from which both the farmer's profit and the landlord's rent are drawn must be smaller. But in remote parts of the country the rate of profit, as has already been shown, is generally higher than near a large town. A smaller share of this reduced surplus, therefore, must go to the landlord.

Good roads, canals, and navigable rivers, by reducing the cost of carriage, bring the remote parts of the country more nearly onto a level with those near the town. For that reason they are the greatest of all improvements. They encourage the cultivation of remote districts, which must always make up the widest circle of the country. They benefit the town by breaking down the monopoly held by the countryside in its immediate neighbourhood. They even benefit that immediate countryside. Though they bring some rival goods into the old market, they also open many new markets to its produce. Monopoly, moreover, is a great enemy of good management, which can only become universal through the free and general competition that forces everyone to adopt it in self-defence. It is no more than fifty years ago that some of the counties near London petitioned Parliament against extending the turnpike roads into the more distant counties. Those remoter counties, they claimed, would be able, thanks to cheaper labour, to undersell them with grass and corn in the London market, and so would cut their rents and ruin their farming. Yet their rents have risen, and their farming has improved, since that time.

A cornfield of moderate fertility produces far more food for human beings than the best pasture of the same size. Its cultivation requires much more labour, but the surplus left after replacing the seed and supporting all that labour is likewise much greater. So even if a pound of butcher's meat were never reckoned worth more than a pound of bread, this larger surplus would everywhere be of greater value and would form a larger fund for both the farmer's profit and the landlord's rent. It seems to have done so everywhere in the crude early stages of farming.

But the relative values of these two kinds of food, bread and butcher's meat, differ greatly at different stages of agriculture. In its crude beginnings, the unimproved wilds, which then make up by far the greater part of the country, are all given over to cattle. There is more butcher's meat than bread, so bread is the food most competed for and consequently fetches the highest price. At Buenos Aires, Ulloa tells us, four reals, twenty-one and a half pence sterling, was forty or fifty years ago the usual price of an ox chosen from a herd of two or three hundred. He says nothing about the price of bread, probably because he found nothing remarkable about it. An ox there, he says, costs little more than the labour of catching it. But corn cannot be grown anywhere without a great deal of labour, and in a country lying on the River Plate, at that time the direct route from Europe to the silver mines of Potosi, the money price of labour could be very cheap. It is otherwise once cultivation has spread over the greater part of the country. Then there is more bread than butcher's meat. The competition shifts direction, and the price of butcher's meat comes to exceed that of bread.

As cultivation spreads, moreover, the unimproved wilds become too small to meet the demand for butcher's meat. A large part of the cultivated land must be used for rearing and fattening cattle, so their price must be enough to pay not only the labour of tending them but also the rent the landlord and the profit the farmer could have drawn from such land used for tillage. Cattle reared on the most uncultivated moors, when brought to the same market, sell, in proportion to their weight or quality, at the same price as those reared on the most improved land. The owners of those moors gain by this and raise the rent of their land in proportion to the price of their cattle. It is no more than a century ago that in many parts of the Scottish Highlands butcher's meat was as cheap as, or cheaper than, even oatmeal bread. The Union opened the English market to Highland cattle. Their usual price is now about three times what it was at the start of the century, and the rents of many Highland estates have tripled or quadrupled in the same period. In almost every part of Great Britain a pound of the best butcher's meat is now generally worth more than two pounds of the best white bread, and in plentiful years it is sometimes worth three or four pounds.

In this way, as improvement advances, the rent and profit of unimproved pasture come to be governed to some extent by the rent and profit of improved pasture, and these in turn by the rent and profit of corn. Corn is an annual crop; butcher's meat is a crop that takes four or five years to grow. Since an acre of land therefore produces far less of the one kind of food than of the other, the smaller quantity must be made up for by the higher price. If it were more than made up for, more cornland would be turned into pasture; and if it were not made up for at all, part of what was in pasture would be brought back into corn.

This equality, however, between the rent and profit of grass and those of corn, between land whose immediate produce is food for cattle and land whose immediate produce is food for men, must be understood to hold only across the greater part of the improved land of a large country. In some particular local situations it is quite otherwise, and the rent and profit of grass are far higher than anything corn can yield.

Thus, near a great town, the demand for milk and for fodder for horses often combines with the high price of butcher's meat to raise the value of grass above what might be called its natural ratio to that of corn. This local advantage obviously cannot be passed on to land farther away.

Particular circumstances have sometimes made certain countries so densely populated that the whole territory, like the land near a great town, has not been enough to produce both the grass and the corn needed to feed the inhabitants. Their land has therefore been used mainly to produce grass, the bulkier commodity and the one that cannot so easily be brought from a great distance, while corn, the food of the bulk of the people, has been mostly imported from abroad. Holland is in this situation today, and a large part of ancient Italy seems to have been so during the prosperity of the Romans. To graze land well, old Cato said, as Cicero reports, was the first and most profitable thing in managing a private estate; to graze it tolerably well, the second; and to graze it badly, the third. Ploughing he ranked only fourth in profit and advantage. Tillage in that part of ancient Italy near Rome must indeed have been greatly discouraged by the distributions of corn frequently made to the people, either free or at a very low price. This corn came from the conquered provinces, several of which, instead of taxes, were required to supply a tenth of their produce to the republic at a fixed price of about sixpence a peck. The low price at which this corn was handed out to the people must have driven down the price of what could be brought to the Roman market from Latium, the ancient territory of Rome, and so must have discouraged its cultivation there.

In an open country too, where the main produce is corn, a well-enclosed piece of grass will often rent higher than any cornfield nearby. It is convenient for maintaining the cattle used to cultivate the corn, and in this case its high rent is paid not so much out of the value of its own produce as out of that of the cornlands cultivated by its means. It is likely to fall if the neighbouring lands are ever fully enclosed. The present high rent of enclosed land in Scotland seems due to the scarcity of enclosure, and will probably last no longer than that scarcity does. The advantage of enclosure is greater for pasture than for corn. It saves the labour of guarding the cattle, which also feed better when not disturbed by a keeper or his dog.

But where there is no local advantage of this kind, the rent and profit of corn, or of whatever else is the common vegetable food of the people, must naturally govern, on land fit for producing it, the rent and profit of pasture.

The use of artificial grasses, turnips, carrots, cabbages, and the other devices found for making a given area of land feed more cattle than it could in natural grass might be expected to reduce somewhat the advantage that, in an improved country, the price of butcher's meat naturally has over that of bread. It seems in fact to have done so; and there is some reason to think that, at least in the London market, the price of butcher's meat relative to that of bread is now a good deal lower than it was at the start of the last century.

In the appendix to his life of Prince Henry, Dr Birch gives an account of the prices of butcher's meat as commonly paid by that prince. He records that the four quarters of an ox, weighing six hundred pounds, usually cost him about nine pounds ten shillings, that is thirty-one shillings and eightpence per hundred pounds in weight. Prince Henry died on 6 November 1612, in the nineteenth year of his age.

In March 1764 there was a parliamentary inquiry into the causes of the high price of provisions at that time. Among other evidence to the same effect, a Virginia merchant testified that in March 1763 he had provisioned his ships with beef at twenty-four or twenty-five shillings the hundredweight, which he regarded as the ordinary price, whereas in that dear year he had paid twenty-seven shillings for the same weight and quality. Yet this high price in 1764 is four shillings and eightpence cheaper than the ordinary price paid by Prince Henry; and it is only the best beef, note, that is fit to be salted for such long voyages.

The price paid by Prince Henry comes to 3⅘d per pound for the whole carcass, coarse and choice pieces together; and at that rate the choice pieces could not have sold retail for less than 4½d or 5d the pound.

In the parliamentary inquiry of 1764, the witnesses gave the price of the choice cuts of the best beef to the consumer as 4d and 4½d the pound, and the coarse cuts generally as somewhere between seven farthings and 2½d or 2¾d; and this, they said, was generally a halfpenny dearer than the same kinds of cuts had usually sold for in the month of March. But even this high price is still a good deal cheaper than we can reasonably suppose the ordinary retail price to have been in Prince Henry's time.
During the first twelve years of the last century, the average price of the best wheat at the Windsor market was £1 18s 3½d the quarter of nine Winchester bushels.
But in the twelve years up to and including 1764, the average price of the same measure of the best wheat at the same market was £2 1s 9½d.
In the first twelve years of the last century, then, wheat appears to have been a good deal cheaper, and butcher's meat a good deal dearer, than in the twelve years up to and including 1764.

In all large countries, most of the cultivated land is used to produce either food for men or food for cattle. The rent and profit of these govern the rent and profit of all other cultivated land. If any particular crop yielded less, the land would soon be turned over to corn or pasture; and if any yielded more, some of the land in corn or pasture would soon be turned over to that crop.

Those crops, indeed, that require either a greater initial outlay to improve the land for them or a greater yearly outlay to cultivate them commonly seem to yield, the one a higher rent, the other a higher profit, than corn or pasture. But this advantage will seldom turn out to amount to more than a reasonable interest on, or compensation for, the extra expense.

In a hop garden, a fruit garden, or a kitchen garden, both the landlord's rent and the farmer's profit are generally higher than in a corn or grass field. But bringing the ground into this condition costs more, so a higher rent becomes due to the landlord. It also calls for more careful and skilful management, so a higher profit becomes due to the farmer. The crop, too, at least in the hop and fruit garden, is more uncertain. Its price must therefore, besides covering all occasional losses, yield something like the profit of insurance. The circumstances of gardeners, generally modest and never more than moderate, may convince us that their great skill is not usually overpaid. Their delightful art is practised by so many rich people for amusement that little money is to be made by those who practise it for profit, because the very people who ought naturally to be their best customers supply themselves with all their most prized produce.

The advantage a landlord gets from such improvements seems never to have been greater than what was enough to cover the original cost of making them. In ancient farming, after the vineyard, a well-watered kitchen garden seems to have been the part of the farm thought to yield the most valuable produce. But Democritus, who wrote on farming about two thousand years ago and was regarded by the ancients as one of the founders of the art, thought it unwise to enclose a kitchen garden. The profit, he said, would not cover the cost of a stone wall; and bricks (sun-dried bricks, I suppose he meant) crumbled in the rain and the winter storms and needed constant repair. Columella, who reports this opinion of Democritus, does not dispute it but proposes a very economical way of enclosing with a hedge of brambles and briars, which he says he had found by experience to be both lasting and impenetrable, though it seems this was not commonly known in Democritus's time. Palladius adopts Columella's view, which Varro had recommended before. In the judgment of those ancient improvers, the produce of a kitchen garden had apparently been little more than enough to pay for the extra cultivation and the cost of watering; for in countries so near the sun it was thought proper, then as now, to have command of a stream of water that could be led to every bed in the garden. Across most of Europe, a kitchen garden is still not thought to deserve a better enclosure than the one Columella recommended. In Great Britain and some other northern countries, the finer fruits cannot be brought to perfection without the help of a wall. Their price in such countries must therefore be enough to cover the cost of building and maintaining what they cannot do without. The fruit-wall often surrounds the kitchen garden, which thus enjoys the benefit of an enclosure that its own produce could seldom pay for.

That the vineyard, when properly planted and brought to perfection, was the most valuable part of the farm seems to have been an unquestioned maxim in ancient agriculture, as it is in modern agriculture throughout all the wine countries. But whether it was worthwhile to plant a new vineyard was a matter of dispute among the ancient Italian farmers, as we learn from Columella. He decides, like a true lover of every curious kind of cultivation, in favour of the vineyard, and tries to show, by comparing profit and expense, that it was a most advantageous improvement. Such comparisons of the profit and expense of new projects, however, are commonly very misleading, and nowhere more so than in agriculture. Had the gain actually made from such plantings been commonly as great as he imagined it could be, there could have been no dispute about it. The same point is still often a matter of controversy in the wine countries today. Their agricultural writers, indeed, being lovers and promoters of intensive cultivation, generally seem inclined to decide with Columella in favour of the vineyard. In France, the eagerness of the owners of old vineyards to prevent the planting of any new ones seems to support their view and to show that those who must have the experience are aware that this kind of cultivation is at present more profitable in that country than any other. At the same time, however, it seems to point to another opinion, that this greater profit can last no longer than the laws that at present restrict the free planting of vines. In 1731 those owners obtained an order of council forbidding both the planting of new vineyards and the renewal of old ones whose cultivation had been interrupted for two years, without special permission from the king, to be granted only after a report from the provincial intendant certifying that he had examined the land and found it incapable of any other crop. The stated reason for this order was the scarcity of corn and pasture and the glut of wine.
