The bank price, or the credit the bank gives for deposits of such silver (when made in foreign coin of well-known and certain fineness, such as Mexico dollars), is twenty-two guilders the mark; the mint price is about twenty-three guilders; and the market price runs from twenty-three guilders six stivers to twenty-three guilders sixteen stivers, or from two to three per cent above the mint price.
The following are the prices at which the bank of Amsterdam at present {September 1775} receives bullion and coin of various kinds:

SILVER — Mexico dollars ................. 22 Guilders / mark; French crowns .................. 22; English silver coin ............. 22; Mexico dollars, new coin ........ 21 10; Ducatoons ....................... 3 0; Rix-dollars ..................... 2 8
Bar silver containing eleven-twelfths fine silver, 21 Guilders / mark, and in this proportion down to one-quarter fine, on which 5 guilders are given. Fine bars ................. 28 Guilders / mark.

Bar or ingot gold is received in proportion to its fineness, judged against the foreign gold coin listed above. On fine bars the bank gives 340 per mark. In general, though, something more is given for coin of known fineness than for gold and silver bars, whose fineness can be determined only by melting and assaying.

The ratios between the bank price, the mint price, and the market price of gold bullion are nearly the same. A person can generally sell his receipt for the difference between the mint price of bullion and the market price. A receipt for bullion is almost always worth something, so it very rarely happens that anyone lets his receipts lapse, or lets his bullion fall to the bank at the price at which it was received — either by failing to take it out before the six months are up, or by neglecting to pay the one-quarter or one-half per cent needed to obtain a fresh receipt for another six months. This does happen sometimes, however rarely, and more often with gold than with silver, because of the higher warehouse rent paid for keeping the more precious metal.

A man who deposits bullion gets both a bank credit and a receipt. He pays his bills of exchange as they fall due with his bank credit, and either sells or holds his receipt depending on whether he expects the price of bullion to rise or fall. The receipt and the bank credit rarely stay long in the same hands, and there is no need for them to. A man who holds a receipt and wants to draw out bullion can always find plenty of bank credits, or bank money, to buy at the going price; and a man who holds bank money and wants to draw out bullion can always find receipts in equal abundance.

The owners of bank credits and the holders of receipts form two distinct kinds of creditors against the bank. The holder of a receipt cannot draw out the bullion it covers without handing back to the bank a sum of bank money equal to the price at which the bullion was received. If he has no bank money of his own, he must buy it from those who do. The owner of bank money cannot draw out bullion without presenting to the bank receipts for the amount he wants. If he has none of his own, he must buy them from those who do. When the holder of a receipt buys bank money, he is buying the power to take out a quantity of bullion whose mint price is five per cent above the bank price. So the five-per-cent agio he commonly pays for it is paid not for an imaginary value but for a real one. When the owner of bank money buys a receipt, he is buying the power to take out a quantity of bullion whose market price is commonly two or three per cent above the mint price. So what he pays for it is likewise paid for a real value. The price of the receipt and the price of the bank money together make up the full value or price of the bullion.

On deposits of the country's ordinary coin, the bank grants receipts as well as bank credits, but these receipts are often worthless and will fetch no price in the market. On ducatoons, for example, which pass in the currency for three guilders three stivers each, the bank gives a credit of only three guilders, or five per cent below their current value. It also grants a receipt entitling the bearer to take out the number of ducatoons deposited at any time within six months, on paying one-quarter per cent for the keeping. This receipt will often fetch no price in the market. Three guilders of bank money generally sell in the market for three guilders three stivers — the full value of the ducatoons if they were taken out of the bank; and before they can be taken out, one-quarter per cent must be paid for the keeping, which would be pure loss to the holder of the receipt. If the bank's agio should ever fall to three per cent, such receipts might fetch some price and sell for one and three-quarters per cent. But since the agio now generally runs about five per cent, such receipts are often left to lapse, or, as they say, to fall to the bank. The receipts given for deposits of gold ducats fall to it still more often, because a higher warehouse rent — one-half per cent — must be paid for keeping them before they can be taken out again. The five per cent the bank gains when deposits of either coin or bullion are allowed to fall to it may be regarded as the warehouse rent for keeping such deposits permanently.

The sum of bank money whose receipts have lapsed must be very large. It must include the bank's whole original capital, which is generally supposed to have stayed there ever since it was first deposited, nobody caring either to renew his receipt or to take out his deposit, since, for the reasons already given, neither could be done without loss. But whatever the size of this sum, the share it forms of the whole mass of bank money is thought to be very small. For many years past the bank of Amsterdam has been Europe's great warehouse for bullion, whose receipts are very rarely allowed to lapse, or, as they say, to fall to the bank. By far the greater part of the bank money — that is, of the credits on the bank's books — is supposed to have been created over these many years by such bullion deposits, which the dealers in bullion are constantly both making and withdrawing.

No claim can be made on the bank except by means of a recipisse, or receipt. The smaller mass of bank money whose receipts have lapsed is mixed and merged with the much larger mass whose receipts are still in force; so although there may be a considerable sum of bank money for which no receipts exist, there is no specific sum or portion of it that could not, at any moment, be claimed by some receipt-holder. The bank cannot owe the same thing to two people; and the owner of bank money who holds no receipt cannot claim payment from the bank until he buys one. In ordinary, quiet times he has no trouble finding one to buy at the market price, which generally matches the price at which he can sell the coin or bullion the receipt entitles him to take out of the bank.

It might be otherwise during a public disaster — an invasion, for instance, like that of the French in 1672. With the owners of bank money all scrambling to draw it out and keep it in their own hands, the demand for receipts could drive their price to an outrageous height. The holders of receipts might form wild expectations and, instead of two or three per cent, demand half the bank money credited on the deposits their receipts had been granted for. The enemy, knowing how the bank was set up, might even buy the receipts up in order to stop the treasure from being carried away. In such emergencies the bank, it is supposed, would set aside its ordinary rule of paying only the holders of receipts. The receipt-holders who held no bank money would have received within two or three per cent of the value of the deposit their respective receipts were granted for. So the bank, it is said, would in this case not hesitate to pay, in money or bullion, the full value credited in its books to the owners of bank money who could get no receipts — while paying two or three per cent to those receipt-holders who held no bank money, that being the whole value justly supposed due to them in such circumstances.

Even in ordinary, quiet times it is in the interest of receipt-holders to push the agio down, so as either to buy bank money — and therefore the bullion their receipts would then let them take out of the bank — that much cheaper, or to sell their receipts to those who hold bank money and want to take out bullion that much dearer; for the price of a receipt is generally equal to the difference between the market price of bank money and the market price of the coin or bullion the receipt was granted for. The owners of bank money, by contrast, have an interest in pushing the agio up, so as either to sell their bank money that much dearer or to buy a receipt that much cheaper. To check the stock-jobbing tricks that these opposing interests might sometimes produce, the bank has in recent years resolved to sell bank money for currency at all times at a five-per-cent agio, and to buy it back at a four-per-cent agio. As a result, the agio can never rise above five or sink below four per cent, and the ratio between the market price of bank money and that of currency is kept at all times very close to the ratio between their intrinsic values. Before this resolution, the market price of bank money used sometimes to rise as high as a nine-per-cent agio and sometimes to sink as low as par, according to how the opposing interests happened to sway the market.

The bank of Amsterdam claims to lend out no part of what is deposited with it, but for every guilder it credits in its books to keep in its vaults the value of a guilder in either money or bullion. That it keeps in its vaults all the money or bullion covered by receipts still in force — which it may be called upon to pay at any time, and which in reality is constantly leaving it and returning again — can hardly be doubted. But whether it does the same with the part of its capital whose receipts lapsed long ago — which in ordinary, quiet times it cannot be called upon to pay, and which in reality is very likely to stay with it forever, or as long as the United Provinces last — may seem more doubtful. At Amsterdam, however, no article of faith is more firmly held than that for every guilder circulating as bank money there is a matching guilder in gold or silver to be found in the bank's treasury. The city guarantees that it is so. The bank is run by the four reigning burgomasters, who change every year. Each new set of burgomasters inspects the treasure, compares it with the books, receives it upon oath, and hands it over with the same solemn ceremony to the set that follows; and in that sober, religious country, oaths are not yet treated lightly. A rotation of this kind seems by itself a sufficient safeguard against any practices that could not be openly admitted. Through all the upheavals that faction has ever caused in the government of Amsterdam, the party in power has never once accused its predecessors of dishonesty in running the bank. No charge could have damaged the reputation and fortune of a disgraced party more deeply, and we may be sure that if such a charge could have been made good, it would have been brought. In 1672, when the French king was at Utrecht, the bank of Amsterdam paid out so readily as to leave no doubt of the fidelity with which it had kept its engagements. Some of the coins then brought out of its vaults appeared to have been scorched by the fire that broke out in the town hall soon after the bank was founded. Those coins, then, must have lain there ever since.

How great the bank's treasure may be is a question that has long exercised the speculations of the curious. Nothing but guesswork can be offered about it. It is generally reckoned that about 2,000 people keep accounts with the bank; and allowing each, on average, to hold the value of £1,500 sterling on his account — a very generous allowance — the whole quantity of bank money, and therefore of treasure in the bank, would come to about £3,000,000 sterling, or, at eleven guilders to the pound sterling, 33,000,000 guilders: a great sum, enough to carry on a very extensive circulation, but far below the extravagant notions some people have formed of this treasure.

The city of Amsterdam draws a considerable revenue from the bank. Besides the warehouse rent already mentioned, each person pays a fee of ten guilders on first opening an account; three guilders three stivers for every new account; two stivers for every transfer; and, if the transfer is for less than 300 guilders, six stivers, in order to discourage a multitude of small transactions. Anyone who fails to balance his account twice a year forfeits twenty-five guilders. Anyone who orders a transfer for more than stands on his account must pay three per cent on the amount overdrawn, and his order is set aside besides. The bank is also supposed to make a considerable profit by selling the foreign coin or bullion that sometimes falls to it when receipts lapse, which is always held until it can be sold at a profit. It profits, too, by selling bank money at a five-per-cent agio and buying it back at four. These various sources of income come to a good deal more than is needed to pay the officers' salaries and cover the cost of management. What is paid for keeping bullion on receipts is alone supposed to yield a clear annual revenue of between 150,000 and 200,000 guilders. The original aim of the institution, however, was public utility, not revenue. Its purpose was to relieve merchants of the inconvenience of an unfavourable exchange. The revenue that has arisen from it was unforeseen and may be regarded as incidental. But it is now time to return from this long digression, into which I have been led almost without noticing, in trying to explain why the exchange between countries that pay in bank money and those that pay in ordinary currency should generally appear to favour the former and run against the latter. The former pay in a kind of money whose intrinsic value is always the same and exactly matches the standard of their respective mints; the latter pay in a kind of money whose intrinsic value is constantly shifting and is almost always more or less below that standard.
Part II — Why These Extraordinary Restraints Are Unreasonable on Other Grounds

In the earlier part of this chapter I have tried to show, even on the principles of the commercial system, how needless it is to lay extraordinary restraints on importing goods from those countries with which the balance of trade is thought to run against us.

Nothing, however, could be more absurd than the whole doctrine of the balance of trade, on which not only these restraints but almost every other regulation of commerce is founded. When two places trade with each other, this doctrine assumes that if the balance is even, neither loses or gains; but that if it tilts at all to one side, one of them loses and the other gains, in proportion to how far it departs from exact equilibrium. Both assumptions are false. Trade forced into being by bounties and monopolies may be, and commonly is, disadvantageous to the very country it is meant to favour, as I shall try to show later. But trade that is carried on naturally and regularly between two places, without force or constraint, is always advantageous to both, though not always equally so.

By advantage or gain I do not mean an increase in the quantity of gold and silver, but an increase in the exchangeable value of the annual produce of a country's land and labour — that is, an increase in the annual income of its people.

If the balance is even, and the trade between two places consists entirely in exchanging their native goods, then in most cases both will not only gain but gain equally, or very nearly so. Each, in this case, provides a market for part of the other's surplus produce; each replaces a capital that had been employed in raising and preparing for market that part of the other's surplus produce, and that had been spread among, and given income and livelihood to, a certain number of the other's people. So some of each country's people will draw their income and livelihood directly from the other. And since the goods exchanged are assumed to be of equal value, the two capitals employed in the trade will in most cases be equal, or very nearly so; and since both are employed in raising the native goods of the two countries, the income and livelihood their distribution provides to the people of each will be equal, or very nearly equal. This income and livelihood, thus furnished to each other, will be greater or smaller in proportion to the size of their dealings. If these came each year, say, to £100,000 or to £1,000,000 on each side, then each would furnish the other's people with an annual income of £100,000 in the one case, and of £1,000,000 in the other.

Suppose instead their trade were such that one of them exported nothing but native goods, while the returns from the other consisted entirely of foreign goods. The balance would still be reckoned even, since goods are paid for with goods. In this case too both would gain, but they would not gain equally; and the people of the country that exported nothing but native goods would draw the greater income from the trade. If England, for example, imported from France nothing but French native goods, and — having no goods of its own that were in demand there — repaid them each year by sending over a large quantity of foreign goods, say tobacco and East India goods, this trade, though it would give some income to the people of both countries, would give more to those of France than to those of England. The whole French capital employed in it each year would be distributed among the people of France; but only that part of the English capital used to produce the English goods with which those foreign goods were bought would be distributed each year among the people of England. The greater part of it would replace the capitals that had been employed in Virginia, Hindustan, and China, and that had given income and livelihood to the people of those distant countries. So if the capitals were equal, or nearly equal, this employment of the French capital would increase the income of the French people far more than the English capital would increase that of the English. France, in this case, would be carrying on a direct foreign trade of consumption with England, while England would be carrying on a roundabout trade of the same kind with France. The different effects of a capital employed in the direct, and of one employed in the roundabout, foreign trade of consumption have already been fully explained.

There is probably no trade between any two countries that consists entirely either in the exchange of native goods on both sides, or of native goods on one side and foreign goods on the other. Almost all countries exchange with one another a mix of native and foreign goods. But the country whose cargoes carry the largest proportion of native, and the smallest of foreign, goods will always be the chief gainer.

Suppose England paid for the goods it imported each year from France not with tobacco and East India goods but with gold and silver. The balance would then be reckoned uneven, since goods would be paid for not with goods but with gold and silver. Yet the trade would, as before, give some income to the people of both countries, though more to those of France than to those of England. It would give some income to England's people. The capital used to produce the English goods that bought this gold and silver — the capital that had been distributed among, and given income to, certain people in England — would thereby be replaced and enabled to carry on the same employment. England's whole capital would be no more reduced by this export of gold and silver than by the export of an equal value of any other goods. On the contrary, in most cases it would be increased. No goods are sent abroad except those for which the demand is supposed greater abroad than at home, and whose returns are therefore expected to be worth more at home than the goods exported. If tobacco worth only £100,000 in England, sent to France, will buy wine worth £110,000 in England, the exchange will increase England's capital by £10,000. And if £100,000 of English gold, in the same way, buys French wine worth £110,000 in England, this exchange will likewise increase England's capital by £10,000. Just as a merchant with £110,000 worth of wine in his cellar is a richer man than one with only £100,000 worth of tobacco in his warehouse, so he is likewise richer than one with only £100,000 worth of gold in his coffers. He can set a greater quantity of industry in motion, and give income, livelihood, and employment to a greater number of people, than either of the other two. But a country's capital is equal to the combined capital of all its people, and the quantity of industry it can keep going each year is equal to what all those separate capitals together can maintain. So both the country's capital and the quantity of industry it can maintain each year must generally be increased by this exchange. It would, indeed, be more advantageous for England to be able to buy French wines with its own hardware and broadcloth than with either the tobacco of Virginia or the gold and silver of Brazil and Peru. A direct foreign trade of consumption is always more advantageous than a roundabout one. But a roundabout foreign trade of consumption carried on with gold and silver does not seem any less advantageous than any other equally roundabout one. Nor is a country with no mines any more likely to be drained of gold and silver by this yearly export of those metals than one which grows no tobacco is to be drained of tobacco by the like yearly export of that plant. Just as a country with the means to buy tobacco will never be long without it, so a country with the means to buy gold and silver will never be long without those metals.

It is a losing trade, people say, that a workman carries on with the alehouse; and the trade a manufacturing nation would naturally carry on with a wine-producing country may be thought of as the same sort of thing. My answer is that the trade with the alehouse is not necessarily a losing one. In its own nature it is just as advantageous as any other, though perhaps somewhat more open to abuse. The work of a brewer, and even of a retailer of fermented liquors, are as necessary a division of labour as any other. It will generally be more advantageous for a workman to buy the quantity he needs from the brewer than to brew it himself; and if he is a poor workman, it will generally be more advantageous for him to buy it little by little from the retailer than in a large quantity from the brewer. He may of course buy too much of either, just as he may from any other dealer in his neighbourhood — from the butcher if he is a glutton, or from the draper if he likes to play the fine gentleman among his friends. Yet it is to the advantage of the great body of workmen that all these trades should be free, even though that freedom may be abused in every one of them, and is perhaps more likely to be abused in some than in others. And though individuals may sometimes ruin their fortunes by drinking too much fermented liquor, there seems to be no danger that a nation will do so. In every country there are many people who spend more on such liquors than they can afford, but there are always many more who spend less. It is worth noting, too, that experience suggests cheap wine is a cause not of drunkenness but of sobriety. The people of the wine-producing countries are generally the soberest in Europe — witness the Spaniards, the Italians, and the people of the southern provinces of France. People are seldom guilty of excess in what is their daily fare. Nobody plays the generous good fellow by being lavish with a liquor as cheap as small beer. On the contrary, in the countries that, from excessive heat or cold, grow no grapes — so that wine is dear and rare — drunkenness is a common vice, as among the northern nations and all those who live between the tropics, the Negroes on the coast of Guinea, for example. When a French regiment comes from one of the northern provinces of France, where wine is somewhat dear, to be quartered in the south, where it is very cheap, the soldiers, I have often heard it observed, are at first led astray by the cheapness and novelty of good wine; but after a few months' residence most of them become as sober as the rest of the inhabitants. If the duties on foreign wines and the excises on malt, beer, and ale were all swept away at once, it might in the same way bring on a fairly general but temporary drunkenness in Britain among the middling and lower ranks, which would probably soon be followed by a lasting and almost universal sobriety. At present drunkenness is by no means the vice of fashionable people, or of those who can easily afford the most expensive liquors. A gentleman drunk on ale has hardly ever been seen among us. The restraints on the wine trade in Britain, besides, seem designed not so much to keep people from going, so to speak, to the alehouse, as to keep them from going where they can buy the best and cheapest liquor. They favour the wine trade of Portugal and discourage that of France. The Portuguese, it is said, are better customers for our manufactures than the French, and so should be favoured over them. Since they give us their custom, the pretence runs, we should give them ours. The sneaking tricks of petty shopkeepers are thus dressed up as political maxims for governing a great empire; for it is only the pettiest shopkeepers who make it a rule to deal mainly with their own customers. A great trader always buys his goods where they are cheapest and best, with no regard for any small interest of this kind.

By maxims like these, however, nations have been taught that their interest lies in beggaring all their neighbours. Every nation has been led to look with a jealous eye on the prosperity of all the nations it trades with, and to count their gain as its own loss. Commerce, which ought naturally to be a bond of union and friendship among nations as among individuals, has become instead the most fertile source of discord and ill will. The reckless ambition of kings and ministers has not, during the present and preceding century, been more destructive of Europe's peace than the meddlesome jealousy of merchants and manufacturers. The violence and injustice of mankind's rulers is an ancient evil, for which, I fear, the nature of human affairs can scarcely admit a remedy. But the mean rapacity and monopolizing spirit of merchants and manufacturers, who neither are nor ought to be the rulers of mankind, though it perhaps cannot be cured, can very easily be kept from disturbing anyone's peace but their own.

That it was the spirit of monopoly which first invented and spread this doctrine cannot be doubted; and those who first taught it were by no means such fools as those who believed it. In every country it always is, and must be, in the interest of the great body of the people to buy whatever they want from those who sell it cheapest. The proposition is so plain that it seems ridiculous to take any trouble to prove it; nor could it ever have been questioned, had not the self-interested sophistry of merchants and manufacturers muddled the common sense of mankind. Their interest, in this respect, is directly opposed to that of the great body of the people. Just as it is in the interest of the freemen of a corporation to keep all the other inhabitants from employing any workmen but themselves, so it is in the interest of the merchants and manufacturers of every country to secure to themselves the monopoly of the home market. Hence, in Britain and most other European countries, the extraordinary duties on almost all goods imported by foreign merchants. Hence the high duties and outright bans on all foreign manufactures that could compete with our own. Hence, too, the extraordinary restraints on importing almost every sort of good from those countries with which the balance of trade is thought to run against us — that is, from those against whom national ill will happens to be most violently inflamed.

The wealth of neighbouring nations, though dangerous in war and politics, is certainly advantageous in trade. In a state of hostility it may let our enemies maintain fleets and armies stronger than our own; but in a state of peace and commerce it must also let them trade with us to a greater value, and provide a better market, whether for the immediate produce of our own industry or for whatever is bought with that produce. Just as a rich man is likely to be a better customer to the industrious people in his neighbourhood than a poor one, so too is a rich nation. A rich man who is himself a manufacturer is, indeed, a very dangerous neighbour to all who work in the same line. But all the rest of the neighbourhood — by far the greater number — profit from the good market his spending provides them. They even profit from his underselling the poorer workmen in the same line. In the same way, the manufacturers of a rich nation may no doubt be very dangerous rivals to those of their neighbours. Yet this very competition is advantageous to the great body of the people, who profit greatly besides from the good market that such a nation's large spending affords them in every other way. Private people who want to make a fortune never think of retiring to the remote, poor provinces of a country, but head for the capital or one of the great commercial towns. They know that where little wealth circulates there is little to be got, but that where a great deal is in motion some share of it may fall to them. The same maxim that would thus guide the common sense of one, or ten, or twenty individuals ought to govern the judgment of one, or ten, or twenty millions, and ought to make a whole nation regard the riches of its neighbours as a likely cause and occasion of riches for itself. A nation that means to enrich itself by foreign trade is certainly most likely to do so when its neighbours are all rich, industrious, and commercial nations. A great nation surrounded on all sides by wandering savages and poor barbarians might, no doubt, grow rich by cultivating its own lands and by its own internal commerce, but not by foreign trade. It seems to have been in this way that the ancient Egyptians and the modern Chinese acquired their great wealth. The ancient Egyptians, it is said, neglected foreign commerce, and the modern Chinese, it is well known, hold it in the utmost contempt and scarcely deign to give it the decent protection of the laws. The modern maxims of foreign commerce, by aiming at the impoverishment of all our neighbours, tend — so far as they actually achieve their intended effect — to render that very commerce trifling and contemptible.

It is because of these maxims that the commerce between France and England has, in both countries, been weighed down with so many discouragements and restraints. Yet if those two countries would only consider their real interest, free of mercantile jealousy and national ill will, the commerce of France might be more advantageous to Britain than that of any other country, and, for the same reason, that of Britain to France. France is Britain's nearest neighbour. In the trade between the southern coast of England and the northern and north-western coast of France, the returns might be expected, just as in the inland trade, four, five, or six times a year. The capital employed in this trade could therefore, in each of the two countries, keep in motion four, five, or six times the quantity of industry, and provide employment and subsistence to four, five, or six times the number of people, that an equal capital could in most other branches of foreign trade. Between the parts of France and Britain most distant from each other, the returns might be expected at least once a year; and even this trade would be at least as advantageous as most other branches of our foreign European trade. It would be at least three times more advantageous than the much-vaunted trade with our North American colonies, where the returns were seldom made in less than three years, and often not in less than four or five. France, besides, is supposed to hold 24,000,000 inhabitants. Our North American colonies were never supposed to hold more than 3,000,000; and France is a far richer country than North America, though, because riches are more unequally spread, there is much more poverty and beggary in the one than in the other. France, then, could provide a market at least eight times larger, and, given the greater frequency of returns, twenty-four times more advantageous, than our North American colonies ever did. The trade of Britain would be just as advantageous to France, and, in proportion to the wealth, population, and nearness of the two countries, would have the same superiority over the trade France carries on with her own colonies. Such is the very great difference between the trade that the wisdom of both nations has seen fit to discourage and the trade it has most favoured.

But the very same circumstances that would have made an open and free commerce between the two countries so advantageous to both have caused the chief obstructions to that commerce. Being neighbours, they are necessarily enemies, and the wealth and power of each becomes, for that reason, more alarming to the other; so that what would otherwise heighten the advantages of national friendship serves only to inflame the violence of national ill will. They are both rich and industrious nations, and the merchants and manufacturers of each dread the competition of the skill and energy of those of the other. Mercantile jealousy is roused, and both inflames and is inflamed by the violence of national ill will; and the traders of both countries have announced, with all the passionate confidence of self-interested falsehood, the certain ruin of each as a result of that unfavourable balance of trade which, they pretend, would be the inevitable effect of unrestricted commerce with the other.

There is no commercial country in Europe whose approaching ruin has not, again and again, been foretold by the supposed experts of this system as the consequence of some unfavourable balance of trade. Yet after all the alarm they have stirred up about it, and after all the futile efforts of almost every trading nation to turn that balance in its own favour and against its neighbours, it does not appear that any one nation in Europe has been impoverished by this cause in any respect. On the contrary, every town and country, as it has opened its ports to all nations, instead of being ruined by this free trade — as the principles of the commercial system would lead us to expect — has been enriched by it. Though there are a few towns in Europe that in some respects deserve the name of free ports, there is no country that does. Holland perhaps comes nearest to that character of any, though still very far from it; and Holland, it is admitted, draws not only its whole wealth but a great part of its necessary subsistence from foreign trade.

There is, indeed, another balance, already explained, very different from the balance of trade, which, as it happens to be favourable or unfavourable, necessarily brings about the prosperity or decline of every nation. This is the balance between annual produce and annual consumption. If, as already noted, the exchangeable value of the annual produce exceeds that of the annual consumption, the capital of society must increase each year in proportion to the excess. In this case society lives within its income; and what is saved each year out of that income is naturally added to its capital and employed so as to increase the annual produce still further. If, on the contrary, the exchangeable value of the annual produce falls short of the annual consumption, the capital of society must decline each year in proportion to the shortfall. In this case society's spending exceeds its income and necessarily eats into its capital. Its capital must therefore decline, and with it the exchangeable value of the annual produce of its industry.

This balance of produce and consumption is entirely different from what is called the balance of trade. It could occur in a nation that had no foreign trade at all, but was wholly cut off from the rest of the world. It could occur across the whole globe, whose wealth, population, and improvement may be either gradually increasing or gradually declining.

The balance of produce and consumption may be steadily in a nation's favour even while the so-called balance of trade generally runs against it. A nation may import more than it exports for half a century together, perhaps; the gold and silver that comes in during all this time may be sent straight out again; its circulating coin may gradually wear away, with various kinds of paper money put in its place; and even the debts it owes to the principal nations it deals with may be gradually mounting — and yet its real wealth, the exchangeable value of the annual produce of its land and labour, may, over the same period, have been increasing in a far greater proportion. The condition of our North American colonies, and of the trade they carried on with Britain before the present disturbances began {this paragraph was written in 1775}, may serve to prove that this is by no means an impossible supposition.

chapters.title: OF DRAWBACKS.
paragraphs: Drawbacks.

Merchants and manufacturers are not satisfied with holding a monopoly over the home market; they also want the widest possible foreign sales for their goods. But their own country has no authority in foreign nations, so it can rarely win them a monopoly abroad. As a result, they usually have to settle for petitioning the government for various forms of support for exports.

Of these forms of support, what we call drawbacks seem the most reasonable. A drawback lets the merchant recover, on exporting his goods, either all or part of any excise or inland duty that has been charged on domestic production. This can never cause more goods to be exported than would have been exported if no duty had been imposed in the first place. Support of this kind does not pull a larger share of the country's capital into any particular line of business than would have gone there naturally; it merely stops the duty from driving part of that share away into other lines of business. It does not upset the balance that naturally settles among all the different employments in a society, but instead prevents the duty from upsetting it. In short, it does not destroy but preserves the natural division and distribution of labour in society, which in most cases is worth preserving.

The same can be said of the drawbacks on re-exporting imported foreign goods, which in Great Britain generally make up by far the largest part of the import duty. Under the second of the rules attached to the Act of Parliament that imposed what is now called the old subsidy, every merchant, whether English or foreign, was allowed to recover half that duty on export: the English merchant if he exported within twelve months, the foreign merchant if he exported within nine. Wines, currants, and wrought silks were the only goods not covered by this rule, since they had other and more generous allowances. At the time, the duties imposed by this Act were the only duties on imported foreign goods. The period within which this and all other drawbacks could be claimed was later extended to three years, by 7 Geo. I, chapter 21, section 10.

Most of the duties imposed since the old subsidy are entirely refunded on export. This general rule, however, has a great many exceptions, and the whole subject of drawbacks has become far less straightforward than it was when they were first introduced.

On the export of certain foreign goods that were expected to be imported in quantities far beyond what home consumption required, the full duties are refunded, without even retaining half of the old subsidy. Before our North American colonies revolted, we held the monopoly on the tobacco of Maryland and Virginia. We imported about ninety-six thousand hogsheads, while home consumption was thought not to exceed fourteen thousand. To make it easier to export the large surplus we needed to get rid of, the full duties were refunded, provided the export took place within three years.

We still hold, if not completely then very nearly, the monopoly on sugar from our West Indian islands. So if sugar is exported within a year, all the import duties are refunded; and if exported within three years, all the duties are refunded except half the old subsidy, which is still retained on the export of most goods. Although sugar is imported well beyond what home consumption requires, the surplus is small compared with what it used to be in the case of tobacco.

Some goods, which our own manufacturers are especially jealous of, are banned from being imported for home consumption. They may, however, be imported and stored in a warehouse for re-export, on payment of certain duties. But none of these duties is refunded on that export. Our manufacturers, it seems, are unwilling to see even this limited importation encouraged, fearing that some of these goods might be smuggled out of the warehouse and end up competing with their own products. It is only under these restrictions that we can import wrought silks, French cambrics and lawns, and calicoes that are painted, printed, stained, or dyed, and so on.

We are reluctant even to act as carriers of French goods, preferring to give up a profit for ourselves rather than let those we regard as our enemies make any profit through us. On the export of all French goods we retain not only half the old subsidy but also the second twenty-five per cent.

Under the fourth of the rules attached to the old subsidy, the drawback allowed on the export of all wines came to considerably more than half the duties then paid on importing them; at that time the legislature seems to have aimed at giving more than ordinary encouragement to the carrying trade in wine. Several of the other duties as well, imposed either at the same time as the old subsidy or later, were allowed to be fully refunded on export, namely what is called the additional duty, the new subsidy, the one-third and two-thirds subsidies, the impost of 1692, and the tonnage on wine. All these duties, however, except the additional duty and the impost of 1692, were paid in ready cash on importation, and the interest on such a large sum created an expense that made any profitable carrying trade in this article unlikely. So only part of the duty called the impost on wine was refunded, and none of the twenty-five pounds per ton on French wines, nor any of the duties imposed in 1745, 1763, and 1778. The two imposts of five per cent imposed in 1779 and 1781 on all the earlier customs duties, which were allowed to be fully refunded on the export of all other goods, were likewise allowed to be refunded on wine. The most recent duty imposed specifically on wine, that of 1780, is allowed to be fully refunded, a concession that, given how many heavy duties remain in place, could almost certainly never lead to the export of a single ton of wine. These rules applied to all places where export was lawful, except the British colonies in America.

The 15th Charles II, chapter 7, called an act for the encouragement of trade, had given Great Britain the monopoly of supplying the colonies with all goods grown or manufactured in Europe, and so with wines. In territories with as much coastline as our North American and West Indian colonies, where our authority was always very weak, and where the inhabitants were allowed to carry out their non-enumerated commodities in their own ships, at first to all parts of Europe and later to all parts of Europe south of Cape Finisterre, it is hardly likely that this monopoly was ever much respected; they probably always found ways to bring back some cargo from the countries they were permitted to export to. They did, however, seem to have some trouble importing European wines from the places where they were grown, and they could not easily import them from Great Britain, where the wines were loaded with many heavy duties, a large part of which was not refunded on export. Madeira wine, not being a European commodity, could be imported directly into America and the West Indies, since those countries enjoyed free trade with the island of Madeira in all their non-enumerated commodities. These conditions had probably created the general taste for Madeira wine that our officers found firmly established in all our colonies at the start of the war that began in 1755, a taste they brought back with them to the mother country, where the wine had not been much in fashion before. At the end of that war, in 1763 (by the 4th Geo. III, chapter 15, section 12), all duties except £3, 10s. were allowed to be refunded on wines exported to the colonies, except French wines, to whose trade and consumption national prejudice would allow no encouragement of any kind. The period between this concession and the revolt of our North American colonies was probably too short to bring about any major change in the habits of those countries.

The same act, which in its drawbacks on all wines except French wines so strongly favoured the colonies over other countries, favoured them far less in its drawbacks on most other goods. On the export of most commodities to other countries, half the old subsidy was refunded. But this law laid down that none of that duty should be refunded on the export to the colonies of any goods grown or manufactured in either Europe or the East Indies, except wines, white calicoes, and muslins.

Drawbacks were perhaps originally granted to encourage the carrying trade, which, since the freight on the ship is often paid by foreigners in money, was thought especially well suited to bringing gold and silver into the country. But although the carrying trade certainly deserves no special encouragement, and although the motive behind the institution was perhaps thoroughly foolish, the institution itself seems reasonable enough. Drawbacks of this kind cannot force a larger share of the country's capital into this trade than would have gone there on its own had there been no import duties; they only keep it from being shut out altogether by those duties. The carrying trade, though it deserves no preference, ought not to be barred but left free, like every other trade. It is a necessary outlet for those capitals that cannot find employment in the country's agriculture or manufactures, or in its home trade, or in its foreign trade of consumption.

Customs revenue, far from suffering from such drawbacks, actually profits from them, through the part of the duty that is retained. If the whole of the duties had been kept, the foreign goods on which they are paid could rarely have been exported, and so could rarely have been imported, for lack of a market. The duties, of which only a part is retained, would then never have been paid at all.

These reasons seem enough to justify drawbacks, and would justify them even if the whole duties, whether on domestic produce or on foreign goods, were always refunded on export. In that case the excise revenue would suffer a little, and the customs revenue a good deal more; but the natural balance of industry, and the natural division and distribution of labour, which such duties always disturb to some degree, would be more nearly restored by such an arrangement.

These reasons, however, will justify drawbacks only on goods exported to countries that are entirely foreign and independent, not to those where our merchants and manufacturers hold a monopoly. A drawback on the export of European goods to our American colonies, for example, will not always result in greater exports than would have happened without it. Thanks to the monopoly our merchants and manufacturers enjoy there, the same quantity might often be sent over even if the whole duties were retained. The drawback, then, may often be a pure loss to the excise and customs revenue, without changing the state of the trade or making it any more extensive. How far such drawbacks can be justified as a proper encouragement to the industry of our colonies, and how far it benefits the mother country that the colonies should be exempt from taxes paid by all their fellow subjects, will become clear later, when I come to discuss colonies.

It must always be understood, however, that drawbacks are useful only where the goods for whose export they are given are genuinely exported to some foreign country, and not secretly re-imported into our own. It is well known that some drawbacks, particularly those on tobacco, have frequently been abused in this way and have given rise to many frauds, equally harmful to the revenue and to the honest trader.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: Bounties

In Great Britain, particular branches of domestic industry frequently petition for export bounties, and sometimes they are granted. Supposedly these bounties let our merchants and manufacturers sell their goods as cheaply as their foreign rivals, or even cheaper. A larger quantity will then be exported, the argument runs, so the balance of trade tilts further in our favour. We cannot give our workers a monopoly abroad the way we have given them one at home. We cannot force foreigners to buy their goods the way we have forced our own countrymen to. So the next best plan, people have decided, is to pay foreigners for buying. This is how the mercantile system proposes to enrich the whole country and put money in everyone's pocket by working on the balance of trade.

Everyone agrees that bounties should go only to those branches of trade that cannot survive without them. But any branch in which the merchant can sell his goods at a price that returns his whole invested capital plus the ordinary profit can clearly survive without a bounty. Such a branch stands on exactly the same footing as every other trade carried on without bounties, so it needs one no more than they do. The only trades that require bounties are those where the merchant has to sell his goods for a price that does not return his capital plus the ordinary profit, or where he has to sell them for less than they actually cost to bring to market. The bounty is meant to cover that loss and to persuade him to keep going, or perhaps even to start, a trade whose costs are assumed to be greater than its returns, where every transaction eats up part of the capital invested in it, and which is of such a kind that if every other trade were like it, the country would soon have no capital left.

Notice that the trades carried on by means of bounties are the only ones that can be run between two nations for any length of time in such a way that one of them always and steadily loses, selling its goods for less than it cost to bring them to market. If the bounty did not repay the merchant what he would otherwise lose on the price of his goods, his own self-interest would soon force him to put his capital to some other use, or to find a trade in which the price returned his capital plus the ordinary profit. The effect of bounties, like that of every other device of the mercantile system, can only be to force a country's trade into a channel far less advantageous than the one it would naturally flow into on its own.

The clever and well-informed author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade has shown very clearly that, since the bounty on corn exports was first set up, the value of the corn exported—valued at a fairly low rate—has exceeded the value of the corn imported—valued very high—by far more than the total of all the bounties paid over that period. On the true principles of the mercantile system, he takes this as clear proof that this forced corn trade benefits the nation, since the value of exports surpasses that of imports by far more than the whole extra public expense of getting the corn exported. What he overlooks is that this extra expense, the bounty itself, is the smallest part of what exporting corn really costs society. The capital the farmer used to grow it must also be counted in. Unless the price of the corn, when sold in foreign markets, returns not only the bounty but this capital plus the ordinary profit on it, society loses the difference, and the national stock shrinks by that much. Yet the very reason a bounty was thought necessary is that the price was assumed to be too low to do this.

It has been claimed that the average price of corn has fallen considerably since the bounty was established. I have already tried to show that the average price of corn began to fall somewhat towards the end of the last century and has gone on falling through the first sixty-four years of this one. But if this fall is real—and I believe it is—it must have happened in spite of the bounty, not because of it. The same fall has occurred in France as well as in England, even though France had no bounty at all and, until 1764, generally banned corn exports outright. So this gradual fall in the average price of grain is probably owing in the end to neither regulation, but to that gradual, imperceptible rise in the real value of silver which, in the first book of this work, I tried to show has taken place across the general market of Europe during this century. It seems altogether impossible that the bounty could ever help to lower the price of grain.

As I have already pointed out, in years of plenty the bounty triggers extra exports and so necessarily holds the home price of corn above the level to which it would otherwise sink. That was the openly stated aim of setting it up. In years of scarcity the bounty is often suspended, yet the heavy exporting it causes in years of plenty must often stop, to some degree, one year's surplus from relieving another year's shortage. So in both kinds of year the bounty necessarily tends to push the money price of corn somewhat higher in the home market than it would otherwise be.

I do not think any reasonable person will dispute that, given the actual state of farming, the bounty must have this effect. But many people have believed it encourages tillage, and in two ways. First, by opening a wider foreign market to the farmer's corn, they imagine it raises the demand for that crop, and so its production. Second, by guaranteeing the farmer a better price than he could otherwise expect in the present state of farming, they suppose it encourages tillage. This double encouragement, they imagine, must over a long stretch of years bring about such an increase in corn production that its home price falls far more than the bounty raises it, given whatever state farming has reached by the end of that period.

My answer is that whatever widening of the foreign market the bounty can produce must, in any given year, come entirely at the expense of the home market. Every bushel of corn exported because of the bounty, which would not have been exported without it, would otherwise have stayed in the home market, raising consumption and lowering the price of corn there. Notice that the corn bounty, like every other export bounty, imposes two separate taxes on the people. First, the tax they must pay to fund the bounty. Second, the tax that comes from the raised price of corn in the home market—and since everyone buys corn, in this particular commodity that tax is paid by the whole population. With corn, this second tax is by far the heavier of the two. Suppose that, year in and year out, the bounty of 5 shillings on each exported quarter of wheat raises the home price of wheat by only 6 pence a bushel, or 4 shillings a quarter above what it would have been given the actual crop. Even on this very modest assumption, the great body of the people, on top of paying the tax that funds the 5-shilling bounty on every exported quarter, must pay another 4 shillings on every quarter they consume themselves. But according to the very well-informed author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade, the corn exported amounts on average to no more than one part in thirty-one of what is consumed at home. So for every 5 shillings they pay towards the first tax, they must pay £6 4s towards the second. So heavy a tax on the first necessity of life must either cut into the food of the labouring poor, or raise their money wages in step with the higher money cost of their subsistence. To the extent that it works the first way, it reduces the poor's ability to educate and raise their children, and so tends to hold back the country's population. To the extent that it works the second way, it reduces employers' ability to employ as many of the poor as they otherwise could, and so tends to hold back the country's industry. So the extra corn exports caused by the bounty not only shrink the home market in any given year just as much as they widen the foreign one, but, by restraining the country's population and industry, in the end stunt the gradual growth of the home market itself—and thereby, over the long run, tend to shrink rather than enlarge the total market and consumption of corn.
Still, people have thought that this rise in the money price of corn, by making the crop more profitable to the farmer, must encourage him to grow more of it.

My answer is that this might hold if the bounty raised the real price of corn, so that with the same quantity of it the farmer could support more labourers in the same manner—generous, moderate, or meagre—as labourers are usually supported in his neighbourhood. But clearly neither the bounty nor any other human institution can have such an effect. The bounty can affect only the nominal, not the real, price of corn to any significant degree. And though the tax it lays on the whole population may be a heavy burden to those who pay it, it brings very little benefit to those who receive it.

The real effect of the bounty is not so much to raise the real value of corn as to lower the real value of silver—to make a given quantity of silver exchange for a smaller quantity not only of corn but of every other home-made commodity. For the money price of corn governs that of all other home-made goods.

It governs the money price of labour, which must always be high enough to let the labourer buy enough corn to keep himself and his family—in the generous, moderate, or meagre manner that the advancing, stationary, or declining state of society forces his employers to maintain him.

It governs the money price of all the other raw products of the land, which in every stage of improvement must bear a fixed proportion to the price of corn, though that proportion differs from one stage to another. It governs, for instance, the money price of grass and hay, of butcher's meat, of horses and their upkeep, and so of overland transport—and thus of most of the country's internal commerce.

By governing the money price of all the other raw products of the land, it governs that of the materials of almost every manufacture. By governing the money price of labour, it governs that of manufacturing skill and effort. And by governing both, it governs the price of the finished manufacture. The money price of labour, and of everything produced by land or labour, must necessarily rise or fall in proportion to the money price of corn.

So even if the bounty lets the farmer sell his corn at 4 shillings a bushel instead of 3s 6d, and pay his landlord a money rent in line with this higher money price, it does him little good if, because corn now costs more, those 4 shillings buy no more of any other home-made goods than 3s 6d would have bought before. Neither the farmer's nor the landlord's circumstances improve much by the change. The farmer cannot farm much better; the landlord cannot live much better. On foreign goods this higher corn price may give them some slight advantage. On home-made goods it gives them none at all. And almost all of the farmer's spending, and by far the greater part even of the landlord's, goes on home-made goods.

When the value of silver is lowered by the richness of the mines, and that fall operates equally, or almost equally, across most of the trading world, it matters very little to any one country. The resulting rise in all money prices, though it does not make those who receive the prices truly richer, does not make them truly poorer either. A set of silver plate genuinely becomes cheaper, while everything else keeps exactly the same real value as before.

But when the value of silver is lowered only in one country—because of that country's peculiar situation or political institutions—the matter is very serious, and instead of making anyone truly richer it tends to make everyone truly poorer. The rise in the money price of all goods, peculiar in this case to that one country, tends to discourage every kind of industry carried on within it. It lets foreign nations supply almost every kind of goods for less silver than that country's own workers can manage, and so undersell them not only abroad but even at home.

Spain and Portugal, as owners of the mines, are in the peculiar position of distributing gold and silver to all the other countries of Europe. Those metals ought therefore to be somewhat cheaper in Spain and Portugal than anywhere else in Europe. But the difference should be no more than the cost of freight and insurance; and since these metals carry great value in small bulk, their freight is trifling and their insurance is the same as for any other goods of equal value. So Spain and Portugal would suffer very little from their peculiar situation if they did not make its drawbacks worse through their own political institutions.

Spain by taxing, and Portugal by banning, the export of gold and silver, burden that export with the cost of smuggling, and so raise the value of those metals abroad above their value at home by the full amount of that cost. When you dam up a stream, then as soon as the dam is full, as much water must spill over the top as if there were no dam at all. The export ban cannot keep any more gold and silver in Spain and Portugal than they can put to use—than the annual produce of their land and labour allows them to use in coin, plate, gilding, and other gold and silver ornaments. Once they have that quantity, the dam is full, and the whole inflow that follows must spill over. Accordingly, by all accounts, the annual export of gold and silver from Spain and Portugal, despite these restraints, comes very near to equalling the whole annual import. But just as the water must always stand deeper behind the dam than in front of it, so the quantity of gold and silver these restraints keep in Spain and Portugal must, relative to the annual produce of their land and labour, be greater than what is found in other countries. The higher and stronger the dam, the greater the difference in the depth of water behind and before it. The higher the tax, the harsher the penalties guarding the ban, the more vigilant and severe the policing of the law, the greater the difference in the ratio of gold and silver to the annual produce of land and labour between Spain and Portugal and other countries. That difference is said to be very large, so that one often finds there a lavish display of plate in houses where there is nothing else that in other countries would be thought to match such magnificence. The cheapness of gold and silver—which is the same thing as the dearness of all goods—is the inevitable result of this glut of precious metals, and it discourages both the farming and the manufactures of Spain and Portugal. It lets foreign nations supply them with many kinds of raw produce and almost every kind of manufactured produce for less gold and silver than they can grow or make it for at home. The tax and the ban work in two ways at once. They not only greatly lower the value of the precious metals within Spain and Portugal, but, by holding back there a certain quantity of those metals that would otherwise flow abroad, they prop up the value of the metals in other countries somewhat above what it would otherwise be—and so give those countries a double advantage in their trade with Spain and Portugal. Open the floodgates, and there will soon be less water above and more below the dam, and the level will soon equalize on both sides. Remove the tax and the ban, and as the quantity of gold and silver falls sharply in Spain and Portugal it will rise somewhat in other countries; and the value of those metals, their ratio to the annual produce of land and labour, will soon reach the same level, or very nearly, everywhere. The loss Spain and Portugal might suffer from this outflow of their gold and silver would be wholly nominal and imaginary. The nominal value of their goods, and of the annual produce of their land and labour, would fall, expressed in a smaller quantity of silver than before; but their real value would be the same, and would still maintain, command, and employ the same quantity of labour. As the nominal value of their goods fell, the real value of the gold and silver they had left would rise, and a smaller quantity of those metals would serve all the same purposes of commerce and circulation that a larger quantity had served before. The gold and silver that went abroad would not go for nothing, but would bring back an equal value of goods of one kind or another. Nor would all those goods be mere luxuries and indulgences to be consumed by idle people who produce nothing in return. Since the real wealth and revenue of idle people would not be increased by this extraordinary outflow of gold and silver, neither would their consumption be much increased by it. Most of those goods, and certainly some of them, would consist of materials, tools, and provisions for employing and maintaining industrious people, who would reproduce, at a profit, the full value of what they consumed. Part of the country's dead stock would thus be turned into active stock and would set in motion a greater quantity of industry than before. The annual produce of their land and labour would immediately grow a little, and within a few years would probably grow a great deal, with their industry relieved of one of the heaviest burdens it now labours under.

The bounty on corn exports works in exactly the same way as this absurd policy of Spain and Portugal. Whatever the actual state of farming, it makes our corn somewhat dearer in the home market than it would otherwise be, and somewhat cheaper in the foreign market; and since the average money price of corn governs, more or less, that of all other goods, it lowers the value of silver considerably in the home market and tends to raise it a little abroad. It lets foreigners—the Dutch in particular—not only eat our corn more cheaply than they otherwise could, but sometimes eat it more cheaply than even our own people can on the same occasions, as we are assured by an excellent authority, Sir Matthew Decker. It stops our own workers from supplying their goods for as little silver as they otherwise might, while letting the Dutch supply theirs for less. It tends to make our manufactures somewhat dearer in every market and theirs somewhat cheaper than they would otherwise be, and so gives their industry a double advantage over ours.

Since the bounty raises in the home market not so much the real as the nominal price of our corn—since it increases not the quantity of labour a given quantity of corn can maintain and employ, but only the quantity of silver it will exchange for—it discourages our manufactures without doing any real service to our farmers or country gentlemen. True, it puts a little more money in the pockets of both, and it will perhaps be hard to convince most of them that this is not a very real service. But if that money loses as much in value—in the quantity of labour, provisions, and home-made goods of every kind it can buy—as it gains in quantity, the service will be little more than nominal and imaginary.

There is perhaps only one set of men in the whole nation to whom the bounty either was, or could be, of any real use: the corn merchants, the men who export and import corn. In years of plenty the bounty necessarily caused more exporting than would otherwise have taken place; and by stopping one year's plenty from relieving another year's scarcity, it caused, in years of scarcity, more importing than would otherwise have been needed. It increased the corn merchant's business in both kinds of year; and in years of scarcity it let him not only import a larger quantity, but sell it at a better price, and so with a greater profit, than he could otherwise have made had one year's plenty not been more or less prevented from relieving another year's scarcity. It is among these men, accordingly, that I have noticed the greatest zeal for keeping the bounty going or renewing it.

When our country gentlemen imposed the heavy duties on imported foreign corn—duties that in times of moderate plenty amount to a ban—and when they set up the bounty, they seem to have copied the conduct of our manufacturers. By the first measure they secured for themselves a monopoly of the home market, and by the second they tried to keep that market from ever being overstocked with their commodity. By both they tried to raise its real value, just as our manufacturers had, by similar measures, raised the real value of many kinds of manufactured goods. But they probably failed to notice the great and essential difference nature has set between corn and almost every other kind of goods. When, by a monopoly of the home market or by an export bounty, you let our woollen or linen manufacturers sell their goods for somewhat more than they could otherwise get, you raise not just the nominal but the real price of those goods; you make them equivalent to a greater quantity of labour and subsistence; you increase not just the nominal but the real profit, the real wealth and revenue, of those manufacturers; and you enable them either to live better themselves or to employ more labour in those particular manufactures. You genuinely encourage those manufactures and steer towards them a larger share of the country's industry than would naturally go to them. But when you raise the nominal or money price of corn by similar measures, you do not raise its real value; you do not increase the real wealth or real revenue of our farmers or country gentlemen; you do not encourage the growing of corn, because you do not enable them to maintain and employ more labourers in raising it. Nature has stamped on corn a real value that cannot be altered merely by altering its money price. No export bounty, no home-market monopoly, can raise that value. The freest competition cannot lower it. Across the world in general, that value equals the quantity of labour the corn can maintain; and in any particular place it equals the quantity of labour the corn can maintain in the manner—generous, moderate, or meagre—in which labour is usually maintained there. Woollen or linen cloth are not the standard goods by which the real value of all other goods is ultimately measured and fixed; corn is. The real value of every other commodity is finally measured and fixed by the ratio of its average money price to the average money price of corn. The real value of corn does not change with those swings in its average money price that sometimes occur from one century to another; it is the real value of silver that changes with them.

Bounties on the export of any home-made commodity are open, first, to the general objection that can be made to all the various devices of the mercantile system: the objection that they force part of a country's industry into a channel less advantageous than the one it would naturally take. And second, they are open to the particular objection that they force it not merely into a less advantageous channel but into a positively harmful one, since a trade that can be carried on only by means of a bounty is necessarily a losing trade. The corn-export bounty is open to the further objection that it can in no way promote the growing of the very crop it was meant to encourage. So when our country gentlemen demanded that the bounty be set up, although they were imitating our merchants and manufacturers, they did not act with the full grasp of their own interest that usually guides those two other groups. They loaded the public revenue with a very large expense; they laid a very heavy tax on the whole population; but they did not, to any noticeable degree, raise the real value of their own commodity; and by lowering somewhat the real value of silver, they discouraged the general industry of the country to some degree, and so, instead of advancing, more or less held back the improvement of their own lands, which depend on the general industry of the country.

To encourage the production of any commodity, you would think a bounty on production would work more directly than one on export. It would also impose only one tax on the people, the one they must pay to fund the bounty. Instead of raising the home price of the commodity, it would tend to lower it, and so, instead of laying a second tax on the people, it might at least partly repay them for what they paid towards the first. Yet production bounties have very rarely been granted. The prejudices built up by the commercial system have taught us to believe that national wealth springs more directly from exporting than from producing. Exporting has therefore been the more favoured, as the more immediate way of bringing money into the country. It has also been said that production bounties have proved more open to fraud than export bounties. How true that is, I do not know. That export bounties have been abused for many fraudulent purposes is very well known. But it is not in the interest of the merchants and manufacturers—the great inventors of all these devices—for the home market to be overstocked with their goods, which a production bounty might sometimes bring about. An export bounty, by letting them send their surplus abroad and hold up the price of what remains at home, effectively prevents this. Of all the devices of the mercantile system, the export bounty is accordingly the one they are fondest of. I have known the various undertakers of some particular works privately agree among themselves to pay a bounty out of their own pockets on the export of a certain share of the goods they dealt in. This scheme worked so well that it more than doubled the home-market price of their goods, despite a very large increase in production. The bounty on corn must have worked wonderfully differently if it has actually lowered the money price of that commodity.

Something like a production bounty has, however, been granted on certain occasions. The tonnage bounties given to the white-herring and whale fisheries may perhaps be regarded as somewhat of this kind. They presumably tend directly to make the goods cheaper in the home market than they otherwise would be. In other respects, though, their effects must be admitted to be the same as those of export bounties. Through them, part of the country's capital is used to bring to market goods whose price does not cover the cost plus the ordinary profit on capital.

But although the tonnage bounties to those fisheries do not add to the nation's wealth, it may perhaps be thought that they add to its defence, by increasing the number of its sailors and ships. This, it may be argued, can sometimes be done by such bounties at a far smaller cost than by keeping up a great standing navy, if I may use the phrase, in the same way as a standing army.
Despite these favourable arguments, however, the following considerations incline me to believe that, in granting at least one of these bounties, the legislature has been very badly deceived:
First, the herring-buss bounty seems too large.

From the start of the winter fishery of 1771 to the end of the winter fishery of 1781, the tonnage bounty on the herring-buss fishery stood at thirty shillings a ton. Over those eleven years the Scottish herring-buss fishery caught 378,347 barrels in all. Herrings caught and cured at sea are called sea-sticks. To turn them into what are called merchantable herrings, they must be repacked with extra salt; and in this case it is reckoned that three barrels of sea-sticks usually repack into two barrels of merchantable herrings. So the number of barrels of merchantable herrings caught over those eleven years comes, on this reckoning, to only 252,231¼. Over those eleven years the tonnage bounties paid amounted to £155,463 11s, which works out to 8s 2¼d on every barrel of sea-sticks and 12s 3¾d on every barrel of merchantable herrings.

The salt used to cure these herrings is sometimes Scottish and sometimes foreign, and both are delivered to the fish-curers free of all excise duty. The excise duty is at present 1s 6d on Scottish salt and 10s a bushel on foreign salt. A barrel of herrings is supposed to need about one and a quarter bushels of foreign salt, or, taking Scottish salt, an average of two bushels. If the herrings are entered for export, none of this duty is paid; if entered for home consumption, then whether they were cured with foreign or Scottish salt only one shilling a barrel is paid. That was the old Scottish duty on a bushel of salt, the quantity which, at a low estimate, was supposed to be needed to cure a barrel of herrings. In Scotland foreign salt is used for almost nothing but curing fish. Yet from 5 April 1771 to 5 April 1782 the foreign salt imported came to 936,974 bushels at eighty-four pounds a bushel, while the Scottish salt delivered from the works to the fish-curers came to no more than 168,226 bushels at only fifty-six pounds a bushel. So it appears that the fisheries mainly use foreign salt. On top of all this, every barrel of herrings exported carries a further bounty of 2s 8d, and more than two-thirds of the buss-caught herrings are exported. Put all this together and you find that, over those eleven years, every barrel of buss-caught herrings cured with Scottish salt cost the government 17s 11¾d when exported and 14s 3¾d when entered for home consumption; and that every barrel cured with foreign salt cost the government £1 7s 5¾d when exported and £1 3s 9¾d when entered for home consumption. The price of a barrel of good merchantable herrings runs from seventeen or eighteen to twenty-four or twenty-five shillings, about a guinea on average. (See the accounts at the end of this Book.)

Second, the bounty to the white-herring fishery is a tonnage bounty, tied to the ship's tonnage rather than to her diligence or success at fishing; and I am afraid it has been all too common for vessels to fit out for the sole purpose of catching not the fish but the bounty. In 1759, when the bounty stood at fifty shillings a ton, the whole buss fishery of Scotland brought in only four barrels of sea-sticks. That year each barrel of sea-sticks cost the government, in bounties alone, £113 15s; each barrel of merchantable herrings, £159 7s 6d.
