Third, the kind of fishing for which this tonnage bounty in the white-herring fishery has been given—busses, or decked vessels of twenty to eighty tons—seems not as well suited to Scotland's situation as to Holland's, from whose practice it appears to have been copied. Holland lies far from the seas where herrings are known mainly to gather, and so can carry on that fishery only in decked vessels able to hold enough water and provisions for a voyage to a distant sea. But the Hebrides or Western Islands, the Shetland Islands, and the northern and north-western coasts of Scotland—the regions near which the herring fishery is mainly carried on—are everywhere cut by arms of the sea that run a good way inland and that in the local language are called sea-lochs. It is to these sea-lochs that the herrings mainly come during the seasons when they visit these waters; for the visits of this fish, and, I am assured, of many other kinds, are not quite regular and constant. A boat fishery, then, seems to be the kind of fishing best suited to Scotland's particular situation, with the fishers carrying the herrings ashore as fast as they are caught, to be either cured or eaten fresh. But the great encouragement that a bounty of 30s a ton gives to the buss fishery is necessarily a discouragement to the boat fishery, which, having no such bounty, cannot bring its cured fish to market on the same terms as the buss fishery. The boat fishery, accordingly, which before the buss bounty was very considerable and is said to have employed as many seamen as the buss fishery now does, has now almost entirely decayed. As for the former extent of this now ruined and abandoned fishery, I must admit I cannot claim to speak with much precision. Since no bounty was paid on fitting out a boat fishery, the customs or salt-duty officers kept no account of it.

Fourth, in many parts of Scotland, during certain seasons, herrings make up no small part of the common people's food. A bounty that lowered their price in the home market might do a good deal to relieve a great many of our fellow subjects whose circumstances are far from comfortable. But the herring-buss bounty does no such good. It has ruined the boat fishery, by far the best suited to supplying the home market; and the extra export bounty of 2s 8d a barrel carries most of the buss fishery's catch—more than two-thirds of it—abroad. Thirty or forty years ago, before the buss bounty was set up, the common price of white herrings was, I am assured, 16s a barrel. Ten or fifteen years ago, before the boat fishery was wholly ruined, the price was said to run from seventeen to twenty shillings a barrel. For the last five years it has averaged twenty-five shillings a barrel. This high price, however, may be owing to a real scarcity of herrings off the Scottish coast. I must also note that the cask or barrel usually sold with the herrings, whose price is included in all the figures above, has, since the start of the American war, risen to about double its former price, from about 3s to about 6s. And I must note too that the accounts I have received of prices in former times have been by no means quite consistent; an old man of great accuracy and experience has assured me that more than fifty years ago a guinea was the usual price of a barrel of good merchantable herrings, and this, I imagine, may still be taken as the average price. All accounts, however, agree, I think, that the buss bounty has not lowered the price in the home market.

When the undertakers of fisheries, after such generous bounties have been heaped on them, keep selling their commodity at the same or even a higher price than before, you might expect their profits to be very large; and it is not unlikely that some individuals' profits have been so. In general, though, I have every reason to believe the opposite. The usual effect of such bounties is to tempt rash undertakers into a business they do not understand; and what they lose through their own carelessness and ignorance more than wipes out everything they can gain from the utmost generosity of government. In 1750, the same Act that first gave the bounty of 30s a ton to encourage the white-herring fishery (23 Geo. II, ch. 24) set up a joint-stock company with a capital of £500,000. Over and above all the other encouragements—the tonnage bounty just mentioned, the export bounty of 2s 8d a barrel, and the delivery of both British and foreign salt duty-free—the subscribers were entitled, for fourteen years, to three pounds a year for every hundred pounds they subscribed and paid into the company's stock, paid in equal half-yearly instalments by the receiver-general of the customs. Besides this great company, whose governor and directors were to reside in London, it was declared lawful to set up separate fishing chambers in all the kingdom's out-ports, provided a sum of at least £10,000 was subscribed to each, to be run at its own risk and for its own profit and loss. The same annuity and the same encouragements of every kind were given to these lesser chambers as to the great company. The great company's subscription was soon filled, and several fishing chambers were set up in the kingdom's various out-ports. Despite all these encouragements, almost all those companies, great and small, lost either all or most of their capital; scarcely a trace of any of them now remains, and the white-herring fishery is now carried on entirely, or almost entirely, by private adventurers.

If some particular manufacture really were necessary for the defence of the country, it might not always be wise to rely on our neighbours to supply it; and if such a manufacture could not otherwise be kept up at home, it might not be unreasonable to tax all the other branches of industry to support it. The bounties on the export of British-made sail-cloth and British-made gunpowder may perhaps both be defended on this principle.

But although it can very seldom be reasonable to tax the industry of the great body of the people in order to support that of some particular class of manufacturers, yet in the recklessness of great prosperity, when the public enjoys more revenue than it knows what to do with, granting such bounties to favoured manufactures may perhaps be as natural as any other piece of idle spending. In public spending, as in private, great wealth may perhaps often serve as an excuse for great folly. But there must surely be something more than ordinary absurdity in keeping up such extravagance in times of general difficulty and distress.

What is called a bounty is sometimes no more than a drawback, and so is not open to the same objections as a true bounty. The bounty on exported refined sugar, for example, may be regarded as a drawback of the duties on the brown and Muscovado sugars from which it is made; the bounty on exported wrought silk, as a drawback of the duties on imported raw and thrown silk; the bounty on exported gunpowder, as a drawback of the duties on imported brimstone and saltpetre. In the language of the customs, only those allowances are called drawbacks which are given on goods exported in the same form in which they were imported. When that form has been so changed by manufacture as to fall under a new name, they are called bounties.

Premiums given by the public to artists and manufacturers who excel in their particular trades are not open to the same objections as bounties. By encouraging exceptional skill and ingenuity, they help keep up the rivalry among the workers actually employed in those trades, and are not large enough to draw towards any one of them a greater share of the country's capital than would go to it naturally. Their tendency is not to upset the natural balance of employments, but to make the work done in each as perfect and complete as possible. Premiums, besides, cost very little, while bounties cost a great deal. The bounty on corn alone has sometimes cost the public, in a single year, more than £300,000.
Bounties are sometimes called premiums, just as drawbacks are sometimes called bounties. But in every case we must attend to the nature of the thing, with no regard to the word used for it.
A Digression on the Corn Trade and the Corn Laws

I cannot end this chapter on bounties without remarking that the praises lavished on the law that established the bounty on corn exports, and on the system of regulations bound up with it, are wholly undeserved. A close examination of the nature of the corn trade and of the chief British laws relating to it will sufficiently prove this. The great importance of the subject must excuse the length of the digression.

The trade of the corn merchant is made up of four different branches which, though one person may sometimes carry on all of them, are by their nature four separate and distinct trades. These are, first, the trade of the inland dealer; second, that of the merchant who imports for home consumption; third, that of the merchant who exports home produce for foreign consumption; and fourth, that of the merchant-carrier, who imports corn in order to export it again.

I. The interest of the inland dealer and that of the great body of the people, however opposed they may seem at first, are in fact exactly the same, even in years of the greatest scarcity. It is in his interest to raise the price of his corn as high as the real scarcity of the season requires, and never in his interest to raise it any higher. By raising the price he discourages consumption and pushes everyone, especially the lower ranks, towards thrift and good management. If by raising it too high he discourages consumption so much that the season's supply is likely to outlast the season's consumption and run on for some time after the next crop begins to come in, he risks not only losing a good deal of his corn to natural decay but having to sell what remains for far less than he could have got for it several months earlier. If by not raising the price high enough he discourages consumption so little that the season's supply is likely to fall short of the season's consumption, he not only loses part of the profit he might have made but exposes the people, before the season ends, not merely to the hardships of a dearth but to the dreadful horrors of a famine. It is in the people's interest that their daily, weekly, and monthly consumption be matched as exactly as possible to the season's supply. The inland corn dealer's interest is the same. By supplying them, as nearly as he can judge, in that proportion, he is likely to sell all his corn at the highest price and with the greatest profit; and his knowledge of the state of the crop and of his own daily, weekly, and monthly sales lets him judge, more or less accurately, how nearly they are in fact supplied in this way. Without intending the people's good, he is necessarily led, by regard for his own interest, to treat them, even in years of scarcity, much as a prudent ship's master sometimes has to treat his crew. When he foresees that provisions are likely to run short, he puts them on short rations. Though out of excess of caution he may sometimes do this without real need, all the inconvenience his crew can suffer from it is trifling compared with the danger, misery, and ruin to which a less provident course might sometimes expose them. In the same way, though out of excess of greed the inland corn merchant may sometimes raise his price somewhat higher than the season's scarcity requires, all the inconvenience the people can suffer from his conduct—which effectively saves them from famine at the season's end—is trifling compared with what they might have faced from a more lavish way of dealing at its start. And the corn merchant himself is likely to suffer most from this excess of greed: not only from the general indignation it stirs up against him, but, even if he escapes that, from the quantity of corn it necessarily leaves on his hands at the season's end, which, if the next season proves good, he must always sell for far less than he might otherwise have got.

If it really were possible for one great company of merchants to get hold of the whole crop of an extensive country, it might perhaps be in their interest to treat it as the Dutch are said to treat the spices of the Moluccas—to destroy or throw away a large part of it in order to keep up the price of the rest. But it is hardly possible, even by the force of law, to set up so wide a monopoly over corn; and wherever the law leaves the trade free, corn is of all commodities the least liable to be cornered or monopolized by the power of a few large capitals buying up the greater part of it. Not only does its total value far exceed what a few private men's capitals could buy; but even supposing they could afford to buy it, the way it is produced makes such a purchase quite impossible. In every civilized country corn is the commodity whose annual consumption is greatest, so a greater quantity of industry is employed each year in producing it than in producing any other commodity. When it first comes from the ground, too, it is necessarily divided among more owners than any other commodity; and these owners can never be gathered into one place, like a body of independent manufacturers, but are necessarily scattered through every corner of the country. These first owners either supply consumers in their own neighbourhood directly, or supply other inland dealers who supply those consumers. So the inland dealers in corn—including both the farmer and the baker—are necessarily more numerous than the dealers in any other commodity, and their scattered situation makes it altogether impossible for them to enter into any general combination. If, in a year of scarcity, any one of them found he had a good deal more corn on hand than he could hope to sell at the current price before the season ended, he would never dream of keeping the price up to his own loss and the sole benefit of his rivals, but would lower it at once to get rid of his corn before the new crop began to come in. The same motives and the same interests that would govern any one dealer would govern every other, and would oblige them all to sell their corn at the price which, by their best judgment, was most suited to the scarcity or plenty of the season.

Anyone who studies, with attention, the history of the dearths and famines that have afflicted any part of Europe in either this century or the two before it—of several of which we have fairly exact accounts—will find, I believe, that a dearth has never arisen from any combination among the inland dealers in corn, nor from any cause but a real scarcity, occasioned sometimes, perhaps, in particular places, by the ravages of war, but in the great majority of cases by the fault of the seasons; and that a famine has never arisen from any cause but the violence of a government trying, by improper means, to remedy the troubles of a dearth.

In an extensive corn-growing country with free trade and communication among all its parts, the scarcity caused by the worst seasons can never be great enough to produce a famine; and the scantiest crop, if managed with frugality and economy, will feed through the year the same number of people who are normally fed more amply by a crop of moderate plenty. The seasons most harmful to the crop are those of excessive drought or excessive rain. But since corn grows alike on high and low ground, on land inclined to be too wet and on land inclined to be too dry, the drought or rain that hurts one part of the country helps another; and though in both wet and dry seasons the crop is a good deal smaller than in one better balanced, yet in both, what is lost in one part of the country is to some extent made up by what is gained in another. In rice-growing countries, where the crop not only needs a very moist soil but must at a certain stage of its growth be kept under water, the effects of a drought are far more dreadful. Even there, however, a drought is perhaps hardly ever so universal as to bring on a famine, if the government would allow free trade. The drought in Bengal a few years ago might well have caused a very great dearth. Some improper regulations, some misguided restraints, imposed by the servants of the East India Company on the rice trade, perhaps helped turn that dearth into a famine.

When the government, to remedy the troubles of a dearth, orders all the dealers to sell their corn at what it supposes a reasonable price, it either stops them from bringing it to market—which may sometimes produce a famine even at the start of the season—or, if they do bring it, it enables, and so encourages, the people to consume it so fast that famine must necessarily follow before the season ends. The unlimited, unrestrained freedom of the corn trade is the only effective preventive of the miseries of famine, and it is also the best palliative of the troubles of a dearth; for the troubles of a real scarcity cannot be cured, only eased. No trade deserves the full protection of the law more, and none needs it so much, because no trade is so exposed to popular hatred.

In years of scarcity, the lower ranks of people blame their hardship on the greed of the corn merchant, who becomes the target of their hatred and outrage. So instead of profiting at such times, he often risks being completely ruined, with his warehouses looted and wrecked by their violence. Yet it is precisely in scarce years, when prices are high, that the corn merchant expects to make his main profit. He usually has contracts with certain farmers to supply him, over a fixed number of years, with a fixed quantity of corn at a fixed price. That contract price is set by what is thought to be the moderate and reasonable level—that is, the ordinary or average price—which, before the recent years of scarcity, was commonly around 28s. for a quarter of wheat, and proportionally for other grain. In scarce years, then, the corn merchant buys much of his corn at the ordinary price and sells it for much more. But that this extra profit is only enough to put his trade on a fair footing with other trades, and to make up for the many losses he suffers at other times—both from the perishable nature of the goods themselves and from the frequent, unpredictable swings in their price—seems clear enough from one fact: great fortunes are as rarely made in this trade as in any other. The public hatred that follows it in scarce years, the only years when it can be very profitable, keeps people of standing and wealth from entering it. It is left to an inferior class of dealers; and millers, bakers, meal-men, and meal-factors, along with a crowd of wretched hucksters, are almost the only middlemen who, in the home market, stand between the grower and the consumer.
The old policy of Europe, far from discouraging this public hatred toward a trade so useful to the public, seems on the contrary to have sanctioned and encouraged it.

The Act of the 5th and 6th of Edward VI, chapter 14, declared that anyone who bought corn or grain meaning to sell it again should be treated as an unlawful engrosser. For a first offence he was to be imprisoned for two months and forfeit the value of the corn; for a second, imprisoned for six months and forfeit double the value; and for a third, set in the pillory, imprisoned at the king's pleasure, and stripped of all his goods and possessions. The old policy of most other parts of Europe was no better than England's.

Our ancestors seem to have supposed that people would buy their corn more cheaply from the farmer than from the corn merchant, whom they feared would demand, on top of the price he paid the farmer, an excessive profit for himself. So they tried to wipe out his trade entirely. They even tried to keep any middleman of any sort, as far as possible, from coming between the grower and the consumer; and that was the point of the many restraints they placed on the trade of those they called kidders, or carriers of corn—a trade no one was allowed to practise without a licence confirming that he was a man of honesty and fair dealing. By Edward VI's statute, the authority of three justices of the peace was needed to grant this licence. But even this restraint was later judged too weak, and by a statute of Elizabeth the power to grant it was limited to the quarter-sessions.

In this way the old policy of Europe tried to regulate agriculture, the great trade of the countryside, by rules quite different from those it set for manufactures, the great trade of the towns. By leaving the farmer no customers except either the consumers themselves or their immediate agents, the kidders and carriers of corn, it forced him to act not only as a farmer but as a corn merchant or corn retailer too. With manufacturers it did the opposite: in many cases it forbade them from acting as shopkeepers or from selling their own goods by retail. By the first law it meant to serve the general interest of the country, or to make corn cheap, though perhaps without anyone clearly understanding how that was to be achieved. By the second it meant to serve the interest of one particular group of men, the shopkeepers, who were assumed to be so heavily undersold by the manufacturer that their trade would be ruined if he were allowed to retail at all.

In fact, even if the manufacturer had been permitted to keep a shop and sell his own goods by retail, he could not have undersold the ordinary shopkeeper. Whatever part of his capital he put into his shop, he would have had to withdraw from his manufacturing. To run his business on the same footing as everyone else, he would need the profit of a manufacturer on one side and the profit of a shopkeeper on the other. Suppose, for instance, that in his particular town ten per cent was the ordinary profit on both manufacturing and shopkeeping stock; he would then have had to charge a profit of twenty per cent on every piece of his own goods that he sold in his shop. When he moved them from his workshop to his shop, he had to value them at the price he could have got from a dealer or shopkeeper buying wholesale. If he valued them lower, he lost part of the profit on his manufacturing capital. And when he sold them from his shop, unless he got the same price a shopkeeper would have charged, he lost part of the profit on his shopkeeping capital. So although he might seem to make a double profit on the same piece of goods, in fact, since those goods were in turn part of two separate capitals, he made only a single profit on the whole capital tied up in them; and if he made less than that, he was a loser and did not employ his whole capital as advantageously as most of his neighbours did.

What the manufacturer was forbidden to do, the farmer was in a sense ordered to do: to split his capital between two different uses, keeping one part in his granaries and stack-yard to meet the market's occasional demands, and putting the other into cultivating his land. But just as he could not afford to use the second part for less than the ordinary profits of farming stock, so he could just as little afford to use the first for less than the ordinary profits of mercantile stock. Whether the capital that actually carried on the corn merchant's business belonged to the man called a farmer or to the man called a corn merchant, an equal profit was needed in either case—to compensate the owner for employing it this way, to put his business on the same footing as other trades, and to remove any incentive to switch it for some other trade as soon as he could. So the farmer who was forced to act as a corn merchant could not afford to sell his corn any cheaper than any other corn merchant would have had to in a state of free competition.

The dealer who can put his whole stock into a single line of business has the same kind of advantage as the workman who can put all his labour into a single operation. Just as the workman gains a dexterity that lets him, with the same two hands, do far more work, so the dealer gains so quick and easy a way of conducting his business—of buying and disposing of his goods—that with the same capital he can handle far more business. And just as the one can usually supply his work a good deal cheaper, so the other can usually supply his goods somewhat cheaper, than if his stock and attention were spread across a greater variety of things. Most manufacturers could not afford to retail their own goods as cheaply as an alert, active shopkeeper whose only business was to buy them wholesale and retail them again. And most farmers could afford it even less—to retail their own corn, supplying the people of a town perhaps four or five miles from most of them, as cheaply as an alert, active corn merchant whose only business was to buy corn wholesale, gather it into a large warehouse, and retail it again.

The law that barred the manufacturer from acting as a shopkeeper tried to push this division in the use of capital along faster than it might otherwise have gone. The law that compelled the farmer to act as a corn merchant tried to hold it back. Both laws plainly violated natural liberty, and were therefore unjust; and both were as foolish as they were unjust. It is in every society's interest that matters of this kind should never be either forced or obstructed. The man who spreads his labour or his capital across more lines than his situation requires can never harm his neighbour by underselling him. He may harm himself, and generally does. Jack-of-all-trades will never be rich, says the proverb. The law should always trust people to look after their own interest, since in their own local circumstances they are generally better judges of it than the legislature can be. The law that compelled the farmer to act as a corn merchant, however, was by far the more harmful of the two.

It obstructed not only that division in the use of capital which is so beneficial to every society, but also the improvement and cultivation of the land. By forcing the farmer to run two trades instead of one, it made him split his capital into two parts, only one of which could go into cultivation. Had he been free instead to sell his whole crop to a corn merchant as fast as he could thresh it, his whole capital could have flowed straight back into the land, going to buy more cattle and hire more servants so as to improve and cultivate it better. But being obliged to retail his corn, he had to keep much of his capital in his granaries and stack-yard throughout the year, and so could not cultivate as well as the same capital might otherwise have let him. This law, then, was bound to obstruct the improvement of the land, and instead of tending to make corn cheaper, it must have tended to make it scarcer—and therefore dearer—than it would otherwise have been.

After the farmer's business, the corn merchant's is really the trade that, if properly protected and encouraged, would do most to increase the supply of corn. It would support the farmer's trade in the same way that the wholesale dealer's trade supports that of the manufacturer.

By providing the manufacturer with a ready market—taking his goods off his hands as fast as he can make them, and sometimes even paying for them before they are made—the wholesale dealer lets him keep his whole capital, and sometimes even more than his whole capital, constantly busy in manufacturing, and so to produce far more goods than if he had to dispose of them himself to the consumers directly, or even to the retailers. And since the wholesale merchant's capital is generally large enough to replace that of many manufacturers, this exchange between him and them gives the owner of a large capital an interest in supporting the owners of many small ones, and in helping them through the losses and misfortunes that might otherwise ruin them.

An exchange of the same kind, established universally between farmers and corn merchants, would bring effects just as beneficial to the farmers. They would be able to keep their whole capitals, and even more than their whole capitals, constantly busy in cultivation. When hit by any of those accidents to which no trade is more exposed than theirs, they would find in their regular customer, the wealthy corn merchant, someone with both an interest in supporting them and the means to do it; and they would not, as now, be left entirely dependent on the forbearance of their landlord or the mercy of his steward. If it were possible—as perhaps it is not—to set up this exchange everywhere and all at once; if it were possible to turn the whole farming stock of the kingdom all at once to its proper task, the cultivation of land, withdrawing it from every other use into which part of it may now be diverted; and if it were possible, in order to support and assist this great stock when needed, to provide all at once another stock almost as large; then it is not easy to imagine how great, how widespread, and how sudden the improvement would be that this change of circumstances alone would bring to the whole face of the country.

So the statute of Edward VI, by barring middlemen as far as possible from coming between the grower and the consumer, tried to wipe out a trade whose free practice is not only the best remedy for the hardships of a dearth but the best safeguard against that calamity—since, after the farmer's trade, none does so much to grow corn as the corn merchant's.

The harshness of this law was later softened by several successive statutes, which one after another allowed the engrossing of corn whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 20s., then 24s., 32s., and 40s. the quarter. Finally, by the 15th of Charles II, chapter 7, engrossing or buying corn in order to sell it again was declared lawful for anyone who was not a forestaller—that is, who did not resell in the same market within three months—so long as the price of wheat did not exceed 48s. the quarter, and that of other grain proportionally. All the freedom the inland corn trade has ever enjoyed was granted to it by this statute. The statute of the twelfth year of the present king, which repeals almost all the other old laws against engrossers and forestallers, does not repeal the restrictions of this particular statute, which therefore remain in force.
This statute, however, lends some support to two very absurd popular prejudices.

First, it assumes that once the price of wheat has risen as high as 48s. the quarter, with other grain in proportion, corn is likely to be engrossed enough to hurt the people. But from what has already been said it seems clear enough that corn can at no price be so engrossed by inland dealers as to hurt the people; and besides, 48s. the quarter, though it may count as a very high price, is in scarce years a price that often occurs right after harvest, when hardly any of the new crop can yet have been sold off, and when not even ignorance could suppose that any part of it has been engrossed enough to hurt the people.

Second, it assumes there is a certain price at which corn is likely to be forestalled—that is, bought up to be resold soon after in the same market—so as to hurt the people. But if a merchant ever does buy up corn, whether on its way to a particular market or in that market, in order to resell it soon after in the same market, it must be because he judges that the market cannot be as well supplied through the whole season as it is on that particular occasion, and that the price must therefore soon rise. If he judges wrong and the price does not rise, he loses not only the whole profit on the stock he employs this way but part of the stock itself, through the expense and waste that inevitably go with storing and keeping corn. So he hurts himself far more seriously than he can hurt even the particular people he may stop from supplying themselves on that one market day, since they can afterwards supply themselves just as cheaply on any other market day. If he judges right, then far from hurting the great body of the people he does them a most important service. By making them feel the hardships of a dearth somewhat earlier than they otherwise would, he keeps them from feeling them later as severely as they surely would if cheap prices had encouraged them to consume faster than the season's real scarcity allowed. When the scarcity is real, the best thing that can be done for the people is to spread its hardship as evenly as possible across all the different months and weeks and days of the year. The corn merchant's own interest leads him to try to do this as exactly as he can; and since no one else can have the same interest, the same knowledge, or the same ability to do it so precisely, this most important operation of commerce ought to be left entirely to him—in other words, the corn trade, at least so far as it concerns the supply of the home market, ought to be left completely free.

The popular fear of engrossing and forestalling may be compared to the popular terror and suspicion of witchcraft. The unfortunate wretches accused of witchcraft were no more guilty of the misfortunes blamed on them than those accused of engrossing and forestalling. The law that ended all prosecutions for witchcraft, taking away any man's power to indulge his malice by accusing his neighbour of that imaginary crime, seems to have effectively ended those fears and suspicions by removing the great cause that fed and sustained them. A law restoring full freedom to the inland corn trade would probably prove just as effective in ending the popular fear of engrossing and forestalling.

The 15th of Charles II, chapter 7, with all its flaws, has perhaps done more, both for the plentiful supply of the home market and for the growth of tillage, than any other law on the statute book. It is from this law that the inland corn trade has gained all the liberty and protection it has ever yet enjoyed; and both the supply of the home market and the interest of tillage are far more effectively promoted by the inland trade than by either the import or the export trade.

The author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade has calculated that the average quantity of all kinds of grain imported into Great Britain comes to no more than one part in five hundred and seventy of all the grain consumed. For supplying the home market, then, the importance of the inland trade must be to that of the import trade as five hundred and seventy to one.

According to the same author, the average quantity of all kinds of grain exported from Great Britain comes to no more than a thirty-first part of the annual produce. For encouraging tillage, therefore, by providing a market for the home produce, the importance of the inland trade must be to that of the export trade as thirty to one.

I have no great faith in political arithmetic, and I do not mean to vouch for the exactness of either of these calculations. I mention them only to show how much less important, in the view of the most judicious and experienced people, the foreign corn trade is than the home trade. The great cheapness of corn in the years just before the bounty was set up may perhaps, with reason, be ascribed in part to the working of this statute of Charles II, which had been passed about twenty-five years earlier and had therefore had full time to take effect.
A very few words will be enough to cover all I have to say about the other three branches of the corn trade.

II. The trade of the merchant who imports foreign corn for home consumption plainly adds to the immediate supply of the home market, and so far must be of immediate benefit to the great body of the people. It does tend to lower somewhat the average money price of corn, but not to lessen its real value, or the quantity of labour it can maintain. If importation were always free, our farmers and country gentlemen would probably, taking one year with another, get less money for their corn than they do now, when importation is most of the time effectively banned; but the money they did get would be worth more, would buy more goods of every kind, and would employ more labour. Their real wealth, their real revenue, would therefore be the same as now, though it might be expressed in a smaller quantity of silver, and they would be neither prevented nor discouraged from growing as much corn as they do at present. On the contrary, since the rise in the real value of silver that comes from lowering the money price of corn also lowers somewhat the money price of all other goods, it gives the industry of the country where this happens some advantage in every foreign market, and so tends to encourage and increase that industry. But the size of the home market for corn must be proportional to the general industry of the country where the corn grows—that is, to the number of those who produce something else, and who therefore have something else, or, what comes to the same thing, the price of something else, to give in exchange for corn. And in every country the home market, being the nearest and most convenient, is also the largest and most important market for corn. So that rise in the real value of silver which results from lowering the average money price of corn tends to enlarge the largest and most important market for corn, and thereby to encourage rather than discourage its growth.

By the 22nd of Charles II, chapter 13, whenever the price in the home market did not exceed 53s. 4d. the quarter, the importation of wheat was subject to a duty of 16s. the quarter; and to a duty of 8s. whenever the price did not exceed £4. The first of these two prices has, for more than a century now, occurred only in times of very great scarcity; and the second has, so far as I know, never occurred at all. Yet until wheat rose above this second price it was, by this statute, subject to a very high duty; and until it rose above the first, to a duty that amounted to a prohibition. The importation of other kinds of grain was held back by rates and duties, proportional to the value of the grain, that were almost equally high. These different duties were imposed partly by the 22nd of Charles II, replacing the old subsidy, and partly by the new subsidy, by the one-third and two-thirds subsidy, and by the subsidy of 1747. Later laws raised those duties still further.

The distress that, in scarce years, the strict enforcement of these laws might have brought on the people would probably have been very great; but on such occasions their enforcement was generally suspended by temporary statutes that allowed, for a limited time, the importation of foreign corn. The very need for these temporary statutes is proof enough of how improper the general one was.

These restraints on importation, though earlier than the establishment of the bounty, sprang from the same spirit and the same principles that later produced that regulation. However harmful in themselves, these or some other restraints on importation became necessary as a consequence of that regulation. If, when wheat was either below 48s. the quarter or not much above it, foreign corn could have been imported either duty free or on paying only a small duty, it might then have been exported again with the benefit of the bounty—a great loss to the public revenue, and a complete perversion of the scheme, whose aim was to widen the market for home-grown corn, not for corn grown in foreign countries.

III. The trade of the merchant who exports corn for foreign consumption certainly does not add directly to the plentiful supply of the home market. It does so, however, indirectly. Whatever the usual source of that supply—whether home growth or foreign importation—unless more corn is usually grown, or usually imported into the country, than is usually consumed in it, the home market can never be very well supplied. But unless the surplus can normally be exported, growers will be careful never to grow more, and importers never to import more, than the bare consumption of the home market requires. That market will very rarely be overstocked; but it will generally be understocked, since the people whose business it is to supply it are generally afraid of being left with goods on their hands. A ban on exportation confines the improvement and cultivation of the country to what its own inhabitants' consumption requires. Freedom of exportation lets it extend cultivation to supply foreign nations as well.

By the 12th of Charles II, chapter 4, the exportation of corn was allowed whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 40s. the quarter, with other grain in proportion. By the 15th year of the same prince this liberty was extended until the price of wheat exceeded 48s. the quarter; and by the 22nd, to all higher prices. A poundage was indeed to be paid to the king on such exportation; but all grain was rated so low in the book of rates that this poundage came to only 1s. on wheat, 4d. on oats, and 6d. the quarter on all other grain. By the 1st of William and Mary, the act that established the bounty, this small duty was in effect removed whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 48s. the quarter; and by the 11th and 12th of William III, chapter 20, it was expressly removed at all higher prices.

In this way the export merchant's trade was not only encouraged by a bounty but made much freer than that of the inland dealer. By the last of these statutes, corn could be engrossed at any price for export; but it could not be engrossed for inland sale except when the price did not exceed 48s. the quarter. Yet the inland dealer's interest, as already shown, can never run counter to that of the great body of the people. The export merchant's interest may, and in fact sometimes does. If, while his own country is suffering a dearth, a neighbouring country were struck by famine, it might be in his interest to carry corn there in quantities that would greatly worsen the hardship of the dearth at home. The plentiful supply of the home market was not the direct object of those statutes; rather, under the pretence of encouraging agriculture, their aim was to push the money price of corn as high as possible, and so to keep up, as far as possible, a constant dearth in the home market. By discouraging importation, the supply of that market, even in times of great scarcity, was confined to the home growth; and by encouraging exportation once the price reached 48s. the quarter, that market was not allowed, even in times of considerable scarcity, to enjoy the whole of that growth. The temporary laws—banning the exportation of corn for a limited time, and lifting the import duties for a limited time—to which Great Britain has had to resort so often, are proof enough of how improper her general system was. Had that system been sound, she would not have been so frequently forced to depart from it.

If all nations followed the liberal system of free exportation and free importation, the different states into which a great continent was divided would so far resemble the different provinces of a great empire. Among the provinces of a great empire, freedom of inland trade appears, from both reason and experience, not only the best remedy for a dearth but the most effective safeguard against a famine; and so would freedom of the export and import trade be among the different states into which a great continent was divided. The larger the continent, and the easier the communication through all its parts by land and water, the less any one particular part of it would ever be exposed to either calamity, since the scarcity of one country would be more likely to be relieved by the plenty of another. But very few countries have fully adopted this liberal system. The freedom of the corn trade is almost everywhere more or less restrained, and in many countries is hedged in by such absurd regulations as often aggravate the unavoidable misfortune of a dearth into the dreadful calamity of a famine. The demand of such countries for corn may often grow so great and so urgent that a small neighbouring state, which happened at the same time to be suffering some degree of dearth, could not dare to supply them without exposing itself to the same dreadful calamity. The very bad policy of one country may thus make it, to some extent, dangerous and unwise to establish what would otherwise be the best policy in another. The unlimited freedom of exportation, however, would be far less dangerous in great states, where the growth being much larger, the supply could rarely be much affected by any quantity of corn likely to be exported. In a Swiss canton, or in some of the little states of Italy, it may perhaps sometimes be necessary to restrain the exportation of corn. In great countries like France or England, it scarcely ever can be. Besides, to stop the farmer from sending his goods at all times to the best market is plainly to sacrifice the ordinary laws of justice to a notion of public utility, to a kind of reason of state—an act of legislative authority that ought to be used, and can be excused, only in cases of the most urgent necessity. The price at which the exportation of corn is banned, if it is ever to be banned, ought always to be a very high price.

The laws about corn may everywhere be compared to the laws about religion. People feel themselves so deeply concerned in whatever touches either their subsistence in this life or their happiness in the life to come, that government must give way to their prejudices and, in order to keep the public peace, establish the system they approve of. That, perhaps, is why we so rarely find a reasonable system established with regard to either of these two great concerns.

IV. The trade of the merchant-carrier, who imports foreign corn in order to export it again, adds to the plentiful supply of the home market. It is not, admittedly, the direct purpose of his trade to sell his corn there; but he will generally be willing to do so, and even for a good deal less than he might expect in a foreign market, because in this way he saves the cost of loading and unloading, of freight and insurance. The people of a country that, through the carrying trade, becomes the warehouse and storehouse for supplying other countries can very rarely be in want themselves. So although the carrying trade must lower the average money price of corn in the home market, it would not thereby lower its real value; it would only raise somewhat the real value of silver.

The carrying trade was in effect banned in Great Britain on all ordinary occasions by the high duties on the importation of foreign corn, most of which carried no drawback; and on extraordinary occasions, when a scarcity made it necessary to suspend those duties by temporary statutes, exportation was always banned. By this system of laws, therefore, the carrying trade was in effect banned.

That system of laws, then, which is tied to the establishment of the bounty, seems to deserve no share of the praise heaped on it. The improvement and prosperity of Great Britain, so often credited to those laws, can easily be explained by other causes. The security that the laws of Great Britain give every man, that he shall enjoy the fruits of his own labour, is by itself enough to make any country flourish, despite these and twenty other absurd regulations of commerce; and this security was perfected by the Revolution, at about the same time the bounty was established. The natural effort of every individual to better his own condition, when allowed to act with freedom and security, is so powerful a principle that on its own, without any help, it is capable not only of carrying society to wealth and prosperity but of overcoming a hundred impertinent obstructions with which the folly of human laws too often hampers its working—though the effect of those obstructions is always, more or less, either to encroach on its freedom or to lessen its security. In Great Britain industry is perfectly secure; and though it is far from being perfectly free, it is as free as, or freer than, in any other part of Europe.

Though the period of Great Britain's greatest prosperity and improvement has come after the system of laws tied to the bounty, we must not on that account credit it to those laws. It has also come after the national debt; but the national debt has most certainly not been its cause.

Though the system of laws tied to the bounty has exactly the same tendency as the practice of Spain and Portugal—to lower somewhat the value of the precious metals in the country where it operates—Great Britain is certainly one of the richest countries in Europe, while Spain and Portugal are perhaps among the most wretched. This difference of situation, however, is easily explained by two distinct causes. First, the tax in Spain and the ban in Portugal on exporting gold and silver, together with the watchful police that enforces those laws, must, in two very poor countries which between them import upwards of six million sterling a year, work not only more directly but far more forcibly to reduce the value of those metals there than the corn laws can do in Great Britain. And second, this bad policy is not, in those countries, offset by the general liberty and security of the people. There industry is neither free nor secure; and the civil and ecclesiastical governments of both Spain and Portugal are such as would by themselves be enough to perpetuate their present poverty, even if their regulations of commerce were as wise as most of them are absurd and foolish.

The 13th of the present king, chapter 43, seems to have established a new system with regard to the corn laws, in many respects better than the old one, but in one or two respects perhaps not quite so good.

By this statute the high duties on importation for home consumption are removed as soon as the price of middling wheat rises to 48s. the quarter; that of middling rye, pease, or beans to 32s.; that of barley to 24s.; and that of oats to 16s. In their place a small duty is imposed of only 6d. on the quarter of wheat, and on other grain in proportion. For all these different kinds of grain, but particularly for wheat, the home market is thus opened to foreign supplies at prices considerably lower than before.

By the same statute, the old bounty of 5s. on the exportation of wheat ceases as soon as the price rises to 44s. the quarter, instead of the 48s. at which it ceased before; the bounty of 2s. 6d. on the exportation of barley ceases as soon as the price rises to 22s., instead of the 24s. before; and the bounty of 2s. 6d. on the exportation of oatmeal ceases as soon as the price rises to 14s., instead of the 15s. before. The bounty on rye is reduced from 3s. 6d. to 3s., and it ceases as soon as the price rises to 28s., instead of the 32s. before. If bounties are as improper as I have tried to prove them to be, then the sooner they cease and the lower they are, the better.

The same statute permits, at the lowest prices, the importation of corn for re-export, duty free, provided that in the meantime it is kept in a warehouse under the joint locks of the king and the importer. This liberty, however, extends to no more than twenty-five of Great Britain's ports. They are, though, the principal ones; and there may perhaps not be warehouses suitable for this purpose in most of the others.
So far, this law seems clearly an improvement on the old system.

But by the same law a bounty of 2s. the quarter is given for the exportation of oats whenever the price does not exceed fourteen shillings. No bounty had ever been given before for the exportation of this grain, any more than for that of pease or beans.

By the same law, too, the exportation of wheat is banned as soon as the price rises to forty-four shillings the quarter; that of rye as soon as it rises to twenty-eight shillings; that of barley as soon as it rises to twenty-two shillings; and that of oats as soon as they rise to fourteen shillings. All these prices seem a good deal too low; and there seems, besides, to be something improper in banning exportation altogether at the very prices at which the bounty, which was given to force that exportation, is withdrawn. The bounty ought certainly either to have been withdrawn at a much lower price, or exportation to have been allowed at a much higher one.

So far, then, this law seems inferior to the old system. With all its imperfections, however, we may perhaps say of it what was said of the laws of Solon: that though not the best in itself, it is the best that the interests, prejudices, and temper of the times would allow. In time it may perhaps prepare the way for a better one.

chapters.title: OF TREATIES OF COMMERCE.
paragraphs: Treaties of Commerce

Sometimes a nation signs a treaty agreeing to admit certain goods from one foreign country while barring those same goods from everyone else, or agreeing to exempt one country's goods from duties that it still charges on everyone else's. When that happens, the favoured country, or at least its merchants and manufacturers, is bound to gain a great deal from the deal. Those merchants and manufacturers effectively enjoy a kind of monopoly in the country that treats them so generously. That country becomes a market for their goods that is both larger and more profitable. It is larger because, with rival nations' goods either shut out or taxed more heavily, it absorbs a greater quantity of theirs. It is more profitable because the favoured country's merchants, holding their near-monopoly, can often sell at a higher price than they could if they had to face open competition from every other nation.

Yet however much such treaties benefit the merchants and manufacturers of the favoured country, they necessarily hurt those of the country granting the favour. That country has handed a foreign nation a monopoly against itself, so its own people must frequently pay more for the foreign goods they need than they would if competition were open to all. And since the home country uses part of its own output to buy those foreign goods, that part of its output must be sold more cheaply. When two things are traded for each other, one being cheaper is just the flip side of the other being dearer; they are really the same fact stated twice. So the exchangeable value of the favouring country's annual output is likely to shrink with every treaty of this sort. Even so, this shrinkage hardly amounts to an outright loss; it is only a reduction in the gain the country might otherwise have made. Although it sells its goods more cheaply than it might, it probably still does not sell them below cost, nor, as happens with bounties, at a price that fails to repay the capital used to bring them to market along with the ordinary profit on that capital. The trade could not last long if it did. So even the favouring country may still come out ahead from the trade, just less than it would under free competition.

Some commercial treaties, however, have been thought beneficial on grounds quite different from these. A trading country has sometimes granted a foreign nation this kind of monopoly against its own interest because it expected that, over the whole of their trade, it would sell more each year than it bought, with the difference flowing back to it in gold and silver. It is on this reasoning that the commerce treaty between England and Portugal, concluded in 1703 by Mr Methuen, has been so highly praised. What follows is a word-for-word translation of that treaty, which has only three articles.

ARTICLE I. His sacred royal majesty of Portugal promises, in his own name and that of his successors, to admit into Portugal forever after the woollen cloths and other woollen manufactures of the British, just as he did before the law banned them, on one condition:

ARTICLE II. Namely, that her sacred royal majesty of Great Britain shall be obliged, in her own name and that of her successors, to admit into Britain forever after the wines grown in Portugal. At no time, whether Britain and France are at peace or at war, shall anything more be charged on these wines, under the name of customs or duty or under any other heading, directly or indirectly, whether they enter Great Britain in pipes, hogsheads, or other casks, than is charged on the same quantity or measure of French wine, less one-third of that customs or duty. But if at any point this one-third reduction is in any way withheld or undermined, the sacred royal majesty of Portugal shall be fully entitled to ban the woollen cloths and other British woollen manufactures once again.

ARTICLE III. The most excellent lord plenipotentiaries promise, and pledge themselves, that the masters named above will ratify this treaty, and that the ratifications will be exchanged within two months.

By this treaty the crown of Portugal commits to admitting English woollens on the same terms as before the ban, that is, not to raise the duties paid up to that point. But it does not commit to admitting them on any better terms than it gives any other nation, France or Holland, for instance. The crown of Great Britain, by contrast, commits to admitting Portuguese wines while charging only two-thirds of the duty levied on French wines, the wines most likely to compete with them. To that extent, then, the treaty plainly favours Portugal and works against Great Britain.

Yet it has been hailed as a masterpiece of English commercial policy. Each year Portugal receives from Brazil more gold than its domestic economy can absorb, whether as coin or as plate. The surplus is too valuable to sit idle and locked away in vaults, and since it can find no profitable use at home, it has to be sent abroad, despite any ban, and exchanged for something more useful at home. A large share of it comes to England every year, paid either for English goods or for the goods of other European nations that take their returns through England. Mr Barretti was told that the weekly packet-boat from Lisbon carries, on average, more than £50,000 in gold to England each week. That figure was probably inflated. It would come to more than £2,600,000 a year, which is more than Brazil is thought to supply.

A few years ago our merchants were annoyed with the Portuguese crown. Certain privileges that crown had granted them, not by treaty but as a free favour, probably at their request and in return for much greater favours, namely defence and protection from the British crown, had been either broken or withdrawn. So the very people usually keenest to celebrate the Portugal trade were then inclined to paint it as less advantageous than it had generally been assumed to be. They claimed that by far the greater part, nearly all, of this yearly gold inflow was not really on Britain's account but on that of other European nations, since the fruits and wines Portugal sent to Britain each year roughly matched the value of the British goods shipped there.

But suppose the whole inflow really were on Britain's account, and that it came to an even larger sum than Mr Barretti imagines. Even so, this trade would be no more advantageous than any other in which, for the same value sent out, we received an equal value of consumable goods in return.

Only a very small part of this inflow, surely, is used to add each year to the kingdom's stock of plate or coin. All the rest has to be sent abroad and exchanged for consumable goods of one kind or another. But if those consumable goods were bought directly with the products of English industry, England would gain more than by first using that output to buy Portuguese gold and then using that gold to buy the consumable goods. A direct foreign trade in consumer goods is always better than a roundabout one, and bringing the same value of foreign goods to the home market takes far less capital the direct way than the indirect way. So if England had put a smaller share of its industry into making goods for the Portuguese market and a larger share into making goods for the markets where the consumables Britain wants can actually be had, it would have been better off. Obtaining both the gold it needs for its own use and the consumer goods would, this way, tie up far less capital than at present. There would then be spare capital free for other purposes, to set additional industry in motion and produce a greater output each year.

Even if Britain were shut out of the Portugal trade entirely, it would have little trouble obtaining all the gold it needs each year, whether for plate, for coin, or for foreign trade. Gold, like every other commodity, can always be got somewhere or other for its price by anyone with that price to pay. Besides, Portugal's annual gold surplus would still be sent abroad, and if Britain did not carry it off, some other nation would, glad to resell it at its price just as Britain does now. True, buying gold from Portugal means buying it at first hand, whereas buying it from any nation but Spain would mean buying it at second hand and perhaps paying a little more. But that difference is surely too trivial to merit public concern.

Almost all our gold, it is said, comes from Portugal, while with other nations the balance of trade is either against us or only slightly in our favour. But we should bear in mind that the more gold we import from one country, the less we must import from all the rest. The effective demand for gold, like that for every other commodity, is limited in each country to a certain amount. If nine-tenths of that amount comes from one country, only a tenth is left to come from everyone else. What is more, the more gold imported each year from particular countries beyond what is needed for plate and coin, the more must be re-exported to others. And the more that most trifling object of modern policy, the balance of trade, seems to favour us with certain countries, the more it must necessarily run against us with many others.

It was on this foolish idea, though, that England could not survive without the Portugal trade, that near the end of the recent war France and Spain, claiming no offence or provocation, demanded that the king of Portugal close all his ports to British ships and, to enforce the closure, admit French or Spanish garrisons into them. Had the king of Portugal accepted the humiliating terms his brother-in-law the king of Spain offered, Britain would have been relieved of something far worse than the loss of the Portugal trade: the burden of propping up a very weak ally, so unequipped for his own defence that the whole power of England, even if aimed at that single task, could scarcely have protected him for one more campaign. Losing the Portugal trade would no doubt have badly inconvenienced the merchants then engaged in it, who might have needed a year or two to find another equally profitable use for their capital, and in that, probably, would have consisted the whole of the harm England could have suffered from this celebrated stroke of commercial policy.

The large annual import of gold and silver is meant neither for plate nor for coin but for foreign trade. A roundabout foreign trade in consumer goods can be carried on more profitably with these metals than with almost any other goods. Because they are the universal instruments of commerce, they are taken in exchange for all commodities more readily than any other goods. And because they pack great value into small bulk, they cost less to ship back and forth than almost any other merchandise, and lose less of their value in transit. So of all the commodities bought in one foreign country purely to be sold or swapped again for other goods in another, none are as convenient as gold and silver. The main advantage of the Portugal trade lies in how it eases all the various roundabout foreign trades in consumer goods carried on in Great Britain, and though this is not a decisive advantage, it is certainly a considerable one.

It seems clear enough that whatever annual addition can reasonably be supposed to be made to the kingdom's plate or coin would call for only a very small yearly import of gold and silver. And even without any direct trade with Portugal, that small quantity could always be obtained easily enough somewhere or other.

Although the goldsmiths' trade in Great Britain is quite large, by far the greater part of the new plate they sell each year is made from old plate melted down. So the net yearly addition to the kingdom's total stock of plate cannot be great, and would require only a very small annual import.

It is the same with coin. Nobody, I think, imagines that even the greater part of the annual coinage, which for ten years running before the recent reform of the gold coin came to over £800,000 a year in gold, was a net yearly addition to the money already in circulation in the kingdom. In a country where the government pays the cost of coining, the value of the coin, even when it holds its full standard weight of gold and silver, can never be much above that of the same quantity of those metals uncoined, since it takes only the trouble of going to the mint, and perhaps a delay of a few weeks, to turn any amount of uncoined gold and silver into an equal amount of coined metal. But in every country most of the coin in circulation is almost always worn down, or otherwise fallen below its standard. In Great Britain, before the recent reform, this was very much the case: the gold was more than two per cent, and the silver more than eight per cent, below standard weight. Now, if forty-four and a half guineas at full standard weight, holding a pound weight of gold, could buy very little more than a pound weight of uncoined gold, then forty-four and a half guineas short of part of their weight could not buy a pound weight, and something had to be added to make up the shortfall. So the market price of gold bullion, instead of matching the mint price of £46:14:6, stood at about £47:14s, and sometimes around £48. Yet when most of the coin was in this degraded state, forty-four and a half guineas fresh from the mint would buy no more goods in the market than any other ordinary guineas, because once they reached a merchant's till and mingled with other money, they could not be told apart again without more trouble than the difference was worth. Like other guineas, they were worth no more than £46:14:6. Thrown into the melting pot, however, they yielded, with no noticeable loss, a pound weight of standard gold, which could be sold at any time for between £47:14s and £48, in gold or silver, as fit for all the purposes of coin as the metal that had been melted down. There was thus an obvious profit in melting down freshly coined money, and it was done so quickly that no government precaution could stop it. The mint's work, on this account, was rather like Penelope's web: what was done by day was undone by night. The mint was employed not so much in adding to the coin each day as in replacing the very best of it, which was melted down each day.

If the private people who carry their gold and silver to the mint had to pay for the coining themselves, it would raise the value of those metals, just as workmanship raises the value of plate. Coined gold and silver would then be worth more than uncoined. A seignorage, provided it was not excessive, would add its full value to the bullion, because, since the government everywhere holds the sole right to coin, no coin can reach the market more cheaply than the government chooses to allow. If the duty were excessive, though, that is, far above the real cost of the labour and expense of coining, then the wide gap between the value of bullion and that of coin might tempt counterfeiters at home and abroad to flood the market with so much false money that the value of the government's money would fall. In France, however, even though the seignorage is eight per cent, no real trouble of this sort arises from it. The dangers a counterfeiter faces everywhere, if he lives in the country whose coin he forges, and that his agents or correspondents face, if he lives abroad, are far too great to be run for the sake of a profit of six or seven per cent.

In France the seignorage raises the value of the coin by more than the proportion of pure gold it contains. Thus, by the edict of January 1726, the mint price of fine gold of twenty-four carats was fixed at seven hundred and forty livres, nine sous, and one and one-eleventh denier per mark of eight Paris ounces. {See Dictionnaire des Monnoies, vol. ii, article Seigneurage, p. 439, par 81. Abbot de Bazinghen, Conseiller-Commissaire en la Cour des Monnoies à Paris.} French gold coin, allowing for the mint's tolerance, contains twenty-one and three-quarter carats of fine gold and two and one-quarter carats of alloy. So the mark of standard gold is worth only about six hundred and seventy-one livres ten deniers. But in France this mark of standard gold is coined into thirty louis d'ors of twenty-four livres each, or seven hundred and twenty livres. The coining therefore raises the value of a mark of standard gold bullion by the difference between six hundred and seventy-one livres ten deniers and seven hundred and twenty livres, that is, by forty-eight livres, nineteen sous, and two deniers.

A seignorage will in many cases wipe out entirely, and in all cases reduce, the profit of melting down new coin. That profit always comes from the gap between the amount of bullion the common currency ought to contain and the amount it actually does contain. If this gap is smaller than the seignorage, there will be a loss instead of a profit. If it equals the seignorage, there will be neither profit nor loss. If it is larger than the seignorage, there will be some profit, but less than if there were no seignorage. Suppose, for instance, that before the recent reform of the gold coin there had been a seignorage of five per cent on the coinage: melting down the gold coin would then have brought a loss of three per cent. With a seignorage of two per cent, there would have been neither profit nor loss. With one per cent, there would have been a profit of only one per cent rather than two. So wherever money is taken by count and not by weight, a seignorage is the most effective deterrent against melting the coin down, and, for the same reason, against exporting it. It is the best and heaviest pieces that are usually melted or exported, because those yield the largest profits.

The law encouraging coinage by making it duty-free was first passed in the reign of Charles II for a limited time, then renewed by various extensions until 1769, when it was made permanent. To refill their vaults with money, the Bank of England often has to carry bullion to the mint, and the directors probably reasoned that it suited their interest better for the government to bear the cost of coining than to bear it themselves. It was probably to oblige this great company that the government agreed to make the law permanent. But should the practice of weighing gold ever fall out of use, as it is very likely to, given how inconvenient it is, and should English gold coin come to be taken by count, as it was before the recent recoinage, this great company may find that here, as on some other occasions, it has rather badly misjudged its own interest.

Before the recent recoinage, when England's gold currency was two per cent below its standard weight and there was no seignorage, the coin was two per cent below the value of the standard gold bullion it ought to have contained. So when this great company bought gold bullion to have it coined, it had to pay two per cent more for the bullion than the coin was worth once minted. But had there been a seignorage of two per cent on the coining, the common gold currency, though two per cent short of its standard weight, would still have equalled in value the standard gold it ought to have contained, the value of the workmanship making up for the loss of weight. The company would, of course, have had the seignorage to pay; at two per cent, its loss on the whole transaction would have been two per cent, exactly the same as it actually was, and no greater.

Had the seignorage been five per cent and the gold currency only two per cent below its standard weight, the bank would in that case have gained three per cent on the price of the bullion. But since it would have had a five per cent seignorage to pay on the coining, its loss on the whole transaction would again have come to exactly two per cent.

Had the seignorage been only one per cent and the gold currency two per cent below standard weight, the bank would in that case have lost only one per cent on the price of the bullion. But since it would also have had a one per cent seignorage to pay, its loss on the whole transaction would have been exactly two per cent, just as in every other case.

If there were a reasonable seignorage while at the same time the coin held its full standard weight, as it has done very nearly since the recent recoinage, then whatever the bank lost on the seignorage it would gain on the price of the bullion, and whatever it gained on the price of the bullion it would lose on the seignorage. It would therefore neither lose nor gain on the whole transaction, and would be, here as in all the earlier cases, in exactly the same position as if there were no seignorage at all.

When a tax on a commodity is moderate enough not to encourage smuggling, the merchant who deals in that commodity advances the tax but does not really pay it, since he recovers it in the price. The tax falls in the end on the last buyer, the consumer. But money is a commodity in which every person is a merchant. Nobody buys it except to sell it again, and with money there is, in the ordinary way, no last buyer or consumer. So when the tax on coinage is moderate enough not to encourage counterfeiting, everyone advances the tax but nobody finally pays it, because everyone recovers it in the raised value of the coin.

A moderate seignorage, then, would never add to the expense of the bank, or of any other private people who carry their bullion to the mint to be coined, and the lack of a moderate seignorage never reduces that expense. Whether there is a seignorage or not, if the currency holds its full standard weight, the coining costs nobody anything. And if the currency is below that weight, the coining must always cost the difference between the bullion that ought to be in it and the bullion that actually is.

So when the government pays the cost of coinage, it not only incurs some small expense but also forgoes some small revenue it could collect through a proper duty, while neither the bank nor any other private people gain in the slightest from this useless act of public generosity.

Still, the bank's directors would probably be reluctant to accept a seignorage on the strength of a line of reasoning that promises them no gain and only claims to protect them from loss. In the present state of the gold coin, and as long as it is taken by weight, they would certainly gain nothing from such a change. But if the practice of weighing the gold coin should ever fall out of use, as it very likely will, and if the gold coin should ever sink into the same degraded state it was in before the recent recoinage, the gain, or rather the savings, the bank would make from a seignorage would probably be very large. The Bank of England is the only company that sends any considerable quantity of bullion to the mint, and the burden of the annual coinage falls entirely, or almost entirely, on it. If this annual coinage had only to repair the unavoidable losses and ordinary wear and tear of the coin, it could rarely exceed fifty thousand, or at most a hundred thousand pounds. But when the coin is worn below its standard weight, the annual coinage must on top of this fill up the great gaps that exportation and the melting pot keep making in the circulating coin. It was for this reason that, during the ten or twelve years just before the recent reform of the gold coin, the annual coinage averaged more than £850,000. Yet had there been a seignorage of four or five per cent on the gold coin, it would probably, even in the state things were then in, have put an effective stop to both exportation and the melting pot. Instead of losing about two and a half per cent each year on the bullion coined into more than eight hundred and fifty thousand pounds, that is, an annual loss of more than £21,250, the bank would probably not have lost a tenth of that.

The revenue parliament sets aside to cover the cost of coinage is only fourteen thousand pounds a year, and the real cost to the government, the fees of the mint officers, does not usually, I am assured, exceed half that sum. Saving so very small a sum, or even gaining another that could not be much larger, may seem too trifling to deserve the serious attention of government. But saving eighteen or twenty thousand pounds a year, should an event occur that is not unlikely, that has happened often before, and that is very likely to happen again, is surely well worth the serious attention even of so great a company as the Bank of England.

Some of the foregoing arguments and observations might perhaps have fitted better in those chapters of the first book that deal with the origin and use of money and with the difference between the real and the nominal price of commodities. But since the law encouraging coinage springs from those common prejudices introduced by the mercantile system, I judged it more fitting to keep them for this chapter. Nothing could suit the spirit of that system better than a kind of bounty on the production of money, the very thing it supposes to constitute the wealth of every nation. It is one of its many admirable contrivances for enriching the country.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Colonies.
Part I. The Motives for Establishing New Colonies.
The motive behind the first European settlements in America and the West Indies was not as plain and obvious as the one that drove the colonies of ancient Greece and Rome.

Each of the various states of ancient Greece held only a very small territory. Whenever the population of any one of them grew beyond what its land could comfortably support, some of the people were sent off to find a new home in some remote, distant part of the world, since the warlike neighbours pressing in on every side made it hard for any state to expand its territory much at home. The Dorian colonies went mainly to Italy and Sicily, which in the period before Rome was founded were inhabited by barbarous and uncivilized peoples. The colonies of the Ionians and Aeolians, the two other great Greek tribes, went to Asia Minor and the islands of the Aegean Sea, whose inhabitants at that time seem to have been in much the same condition as those of Sicily and Italy. The mother city always regarded the colony as a child entitled to great favour and assistance, and owing much gratitude and respect in return; but it treated it as an emancipated child over whom it claimed no direct authority or jurisdiction. The colony set up its own form of government, passed its own laws, elected its own magistrates, and made peace or war with its neighbours as an independent state, with no need to wait for the mother city's approval or consent. Nothing could be plainer or more obvious than the motive behind each of these foundings.

Rome, like most of the other ancient republics, was originally founded on an agrarian law that divided the public territory in fixed proportions among the various citizens who made up the state.
